subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF REPATRIATION AT CHARLOTTETOWN CONFERENCE

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF REPATRIATION AT CHARLOTTETOWN CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure I speak for all members of the house in welcoming the Prime Minister back following the celebration of the 100th anniversary of that historic gathering at Charlottetown. In saying that I wish to ask him something about the repatriation of the constitution. Has the formula advanced in December, 1961 by the minister of justice in the government of which I had the honour to be the head been accepted, and what modifications in that formula are indicated? I ask him particularly whether there is any foundation for the press articles which suggest that the federal government is prepared to surrender or diminish its right to amend certain sections of the British North America Act relating to matters purely within the federal jurisdiction. I think a statement from the Prime Minister is necessary in order to have the assurance that such is not being contemplated.
I ask the latter portion of the question on the basis of an article in Le Soleil in which the premier of Quebec is quoted as saying that the agreement of the province is subordinated to the abrogation or satisfactory revision of article 91, section 1 of the constitution which, of course, is the one concerning the distribution of legislative powers.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF REPATRIATION AT CHARLOTTETOWN CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the right hon. gentleman for his welcome back to the house after an interesting and agreeable conference at Charlottetown, where the hospitality was almost as openhearted as it was 100 years ago.
So far as this particular question is concerned, I am happy to inform him that as the statement issued yesterday morning indicates, and I am quoting from a paragraph of it now:
The Prime Minister and premiers affirmed their unanimous decision to conclude the repatriation of the British North America Act without delay.
To this end they decided to complete a procedure for amending the constitution of Canada, based on the draft legislation proposed at the constitutional conference of 1961, which they accept in principle.
This acceptance, of course, includes the formula to which my hon. friend referred. Then the next paragraph states:
An early meeting of the attorneys general of Canada and the provinces will be held to complete the amending formula devised by the 1961 conference-
In so far as the specific question he asked is concerned, based on a newspaper report, there is no foundation to the report that the federal government at Charlottetown indicated its willingness to give up its own rights under the proposed legislation in respect of those matters under its jurisdiction which are covered in section 91, subsection 1 of the British North America Act. It was agreed, Mr. Speaker, that at the meeting of the attorneys general to which I have just referred and which is mentioned in the statement, section 91(1) could be examined in order to ascertain if there are any specific matters in that section in which the provinces have a legitimate and direct concern, and if so to decide whether the formula should be applied to the amendment of those particular matters.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF REPATRIATION AT CHARLOTTETOWN CONFERENCE
speechtext: Would the Prime Minister allow me to ask which particular matters he has in mind?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF REPATRIATION AT CHARLOTTETOWN CONFERENCE
speechtext: I have no particular matters in mind. We are quite content to receive from the provinces any information they may wish to send us concerning that which they may think they have a legitimate interest in amending. We will look at it from that point of view, and this will be the purpose of the meeting of attorneys general to be held shortly to see how the particular sections could be adapted to the amending formula which we have agreed upon in principle.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF REPATRIATION AT CHARLOTTETOWN CONFERENCE
speechtext:
May I ask the Prime Minister whether there has been any change in the attitude of the governments of Saskatchewan and Quebec since Mr. Fulton, as minister of justice, advanced the views of the dominion government in December of 1961?

Inquiries of the Ministry
Then I also want to ask him this regarding these questions of legislation in respect of which representation will be made by the provinces. Was there any suggestion that any of the provinces should have the authority to legislate in certain recognized federal fields, such as immigration and the like, or should have any veto power over monetary or tariff policy?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF REPATRIATION AT CHARLOTTETOWN CONFERENCE
speechtext: The answer to the last part of the question is no. In so far as the first part of the question is concerned, the premier of Saskatchewan indicated that the amending formula put forward in 1961, and which at that time was not acceptable to the government of Saskatchewan, is now acceptable to that government. The prime minister of Quebec indicated that the position of his government in respect of section 91(1) was the same as the position taken in 1961, in other words that the application of the formula to that particular section of the British North America Act should be examined before the formula comes into effect.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF REPATRIATION AT CHARLOTTETOWN CONFERENCE
speechtext: So that the position today is that the change since December 1961 is that with a change in government in Saskatchewan the present government has agreed with the formula of 1961, and that so far as the premier of Quebec is concerned he wishes to examine the formula to which objection was taken in 1961?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF REPATRIATION AT CHARLOTTETOWN CONFERENCE
speechtext: That is correct, Mr. Speaker, with this addition; that the head of the government of Quebec, along with the heads of the governments of all the other provinces, now accept in principle the draft formula of 1961, which they had not accepted at that earlier conference.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF REPATRIATION AT CHARLOTTETOWN CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a supplementary question to the Prime Minister.
Has he any comment to make about the statements allegedly made by Messrs. Roblin and Thatcher that an agreement on a formula to repatriate the constitution was still far away.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF REPATRIATION AT CHARLOTTETOWN CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Well, Mr. Speaker, Mr. Roblin, as I understand from the reports, indicated some impatience that we were not able to reach final agreement on all details yesterday in Charlottetown, and I have no comment to make on that. I am not quite

certain what Mr. Thatcher said, but I think he also indicated the same kind of impatience and hope that there could have been final agreement yesterday. We all shared that hope, but the position taken at the conference by all heads of government was a very helpful one, and we hope that in a very few weeks the remaining difficulties will be cleared up.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF REPATRIATION AT CHARLOTTETOWN CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it is a great pity the Prime Minister did not make a statement on motions so we could have had a full statement on the conference in Charlottetown. However, we all welcome him back, and he has our full support in any steps that may be taken to repatriate the constitution.
I want to ask him whether the government is placing its wholehearted support behind the so-called Fulton formula of 1961. Does this mean the government is now committing itself as well as the provinces to entrenching subsection 92(13), the property and civil rights subsection, which would mean that legislative matters having to do with pensions, a labour code and a great many other matters of that sort, under recent decisions by the courts could not be amended without the unanimous consent of the parliament of Canada and all ten provinces? Is this the position the federal government is taking?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF REPATRIATION AT CHARLOTTETOWN CONFERENCE
speechtext: Not necessarily, Mr. Speaker. I am sorry if my hon. friend thought a statement should have been made on motions, but the communique was very short and I thought it would probably be more appropriate if I were asked questions so that other hon. members in addition to the party leaders might ask questions also. I would be glad to make a statement next week, if that is desirable, but so far as the federal details in this matter are concerned I cannot go beyond what I have already said. I do not accept the hon. gentleman's interpretation of our position with regard to entrenchment generally.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF REPATRIATION AT CHARLOTTETOWN CONFERENCE
speechtext: Could I ask the Prime Minister if in view of the wide powers which the courts have injected into the property and civil rights clause he does not consider that entrenching this clause would put Canada in a constitutional strait-jacket for many years to come?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF REPATRIATION AT CHARLOTTETOWN CONFERENCE
speechtext:
I can only say that in recent years, in respect to the amendment of the constitution, Canada has been in a kind of

strait-jacket, a strait-jacket imposed from outside.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF REPATRIATION AT CHARLOTTETOWN CONFERENCE
speechtext: Is it not true that at present the Canadian constitution can be amended at any time by an address of both houses of parliament?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF REPATRIATION AT CHARLOTTETOWN CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Prime Minister a supplementary question.
In the course of his discussions with the provincial premiers about the eventual and desirable repatriation of our constitution, was there any mention made of the title our Canadian constitution should bear in the future, if it is repatriated?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF REPATRIATION AT CHARLOTTETOWN CONFERENCE
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker. While I am on my feet perhaps I could explain that when I said we had been subject to a strait-jacket imposed on us from outside, I should have added that the imposition was of our own doing.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF REPATRIATION AT CHARLOTTETOWN CONFERENCE
speechtext: I realize this meeting was very short, but I should like to ask a question dealing with an aspect of this matter apart from the repatriation of the constitution itself. Would the Prime Minister tell us whether any suggestion was made to hold a federal-provincial conference to modernize and bring up to date the constitution to suit the needs of modern times?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF REPATRIATION AT CHARLOTTETOWN CONFERENCE
speechtext: No. We restricted our discussion to methods of amending the constitution. But I should add that in the discussions just completed we agreed to have another meeting to consider, if possible, a report from the attorneys general on the amendment of the constitution and any other questions which the premiers might wish to bring up. This meeting will be held immediately following the visit of the Queen to Ottawa on October 11. There will be a two day meeting after that between the premiers of the provinces and the Prime Minister.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF REPATRIATION AT CHARLOTTETOWN CONFERENCE
speechtext: Will that be during the presence of Her Majesty the Queen in Ottawa?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF REPATRIATION AT CHARLOTTETOWN CONFERENCE
speechtext: No, it will be the day after she leaves.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF REPATRIATION AT CHARLOTTETOWN CONFERENCE
speechtext:
I should like to ask the Prime Minister this. In view of the major importance of the step to be taken, would he consider setting a day aside very shortly,
Inquiries of the Ministry and before we adjourn this portion of the session, for the purpose of securing the views of the house on this matter? In 1961 there had been discussions from time to time in the house on this question which divides itself into two parts; first, the repatriation of the constitution, which latter I cannot agree is anything in the nature of a strait-jacket; and second, reconsideration of the whole question of the entranchment of powers. Is it the right hon. gentleman's intention to allow the house an opportunity to discuss these matters before anything is finally determined and, in particular, before legislation is brought before parliament?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF REPATRIATION AT CHARLOTTETOWN CONFERENCE
speechtext: Parliament will undoubtedly be required to consider any action before that action can be taken if it deals with a new procedure for amending our constitution, and there would be an opportunity for parliament to do so at the time a decision has finally been reached between the governments of the provinces and the federal government. However, it seems to me it would be quite proper that there should be a general and earlier discussion of this very important matter. Perhaps the estimates of the Department of Justice would be a suitable occasion and, if so, we shall try to expedite them. We could bring them forward next week, perhaps. I am informed-I do not want to mislead the house-that the estimates of the Department of Justice are not in supply yet. Perhaps we could make some special arrangement.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF REPATRIATION AT CHARLOTTETOWN CONFERENCE
speechtext: I should like to ask a supplementary question relating to that asked by the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi a few minutes ago. Does the Prime Minister intend to call another conference later this year between himself and the ten premiers for the purpose of modernizing the constitution after it has been repatriated?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF REPATRIATION AT CHARLOTTETOWN CONFERENCE
speechtext: I think we had better restrict our consideration at the moment to the subject of amending our constitution here in Canada. In addition to the meeting in October, there will be a further meeting with the provincial premiers, the annual meeting held late in November or in December. It is a little early to say what will be on the agenda.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF REPATRIATION AT CHARLOTTETOWN CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wonder whether the Prime Minister would consider setting up a special committee of the house to study this whole question, so that when the measure is before the house hon. members will have something of a preliminary study on this question.

Inquiries of the Ministry

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF REPATRIATION AT CHARLOTTETOWN CONFERENCE
speechtext: I will be glad to give consideration to that suggestion, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF REPATRIATION AT CHARLOTTETOWN CONFERENCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a supplementary question to the Prime Minister. Was there any discussion at Charlottetown, as the Prime Minister said earlier this session, in response to questions, there would be, with respect to how the repatriating of the constitution will be brought about? Will it be by an act of another parliament, or will it be by an act that we take in this our own sovereign parliament?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF REPATRIATION AT CHARLOTTETOWN CONFERENCE
speechtext: That matter was mentioned, but it was not discussed in any detail. It will certainly be considered by the attorneys general and the Minister of Justice. On this particular point, Mr. Speaker, I have nothing to add to the answer I gave to a question put by my hon. friend, I think it was last week, in the house.
On the orders of the day:

Mr. Speaker, my question is to the Prime Minister. Is the Prime Minister in a position to inform the house in regard to the proposal made by the premier of New Brunswick relative to the union of the Atlantic provinces? Would he care to tell the house about this?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker, I do not think I would care to express any opinion on that matter at this time. Surely that is a matter for the four Atlantic provinces. At the meeting at which the proposal was put forward they had some comments to make on it, but I believe they have not given it very serious consideration.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. It is something I very, very rarely do; therefore Your Honour will understand that it is a matter which I feel is of importance concerning myself. I refer Your Honour and hon. members to yesterday's Hansard, page 7581, the first column, starting at line 26, wherein the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre had this to say in reference to myself:
[Mr. ValaUe.l
-I recall him saying that all he would have to do to be re-elected in the next election would be to march up and down carrying the red ensign in his hand.

subtopic: MR. WINCH    REMARKS IN DEBATE BY MEMBER FOR WINNIPEG SOUTH CENTRE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: MR. WINCH    REMARKS IN DEBATE BY MEMBER FOR WINNIPEG SOUTH CENTRE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have at no time been interviewed by the press on my position. I have not as yet spoken in the House of Commons on this flag issue. When I do, that will be my business and my opportunity. However, Mr. Speaker, never having made any such statement in my life, I think I have the right to rise at this time, in view of that statement made yesterday by the hon. member, and say that it is only because of my respect for the House of Commons, its decency and decorum that I say his statement yesterday was a most vicious, despicable inexactitude of terminology.

Hon. Gordon Churchill (Winnipeg South
Centre): Mr. Speaker, I am rising on a question of privilege based on the rather sharp attack made on me by the hon. member for Vancouver East. I want to state that I had no intention of offending the hon. member yesterday, and I was rather surprised that he did not raise some objection when I used the words which he now considers to be offensive, as he was in the house at the time.
May I draw to your attention, sir, that when I rose to speak yesterday he interrupted and left the imputation that I was speaking without authority, that I had participated earlier in the debate and should not be allowed to speak again. This occasioned what I thought was a friendly exchange; but if the hon. member has been offended by any words I used I am quite prepared willingly and publicly to apologize to him, and I wish him all the best in the next election.
On the orders of the day:

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the acting minister of external affairs and relates to the safety and well being of a number of Canadian citizens who are at the present time in the fighting areas of the Congo. Does the minister have any information for the house with respect to the safety of these individuals?

speakeroldname: Hon. C. M. Drury (Acting Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I think all members know, a register is maintained by

our embassy in the Congo of all Canadians resident there. These people have been advised by the embassy from time to time to evacuate danger, or possible danger, areas. Some departures have taken place. In other cases Canadian missionaries have preferred to stay en place. In respect of those who have remained, arrangements have been made, with the generous co-operation of the United States embassy, and with the help of the UN authorities for the rapid evacuation to places of safety of those who may so wish to be evacuated.
On the orders of the day:

Mr. Speaker, I should like to address a question to the right hon. Prime Minister. On Tuesday and again yesterday the government of India sent an urgent appeal to both the United States and Australia to divert shipments of wheat to India because of the severe flood damage that has been occasioned during the past few days. I should like to ask the Prime Minister whether Canada has received an appeal from the government of India for wheat and other foodstuffs and, if so, what is the response to the request.
That question was asked yesterday.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker, this question was asked yesterday by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle. I can only say that no special request has been received from the government of India for special help in this emergency. As the house is no doubt aware, we are supplying to India at the present time about $7 million worth of Canadian wheat, which is an increase of $5,500,000 over the amount supplied in each of the last two fiscal years, and credits for the purchase of additional supplies if required. Part of the $7 million worth of wheat to which I referred was shipped from Canadian ports in August, and the balance is going forward in September. I do not think therefore, Mr. Speaker, that there would be any possibility of diverting wheat at this time in a way which would assist India. We are examining the matter and making inquiries as to whether there is anything in addition to what I have mentioned that we can do to help India in this emergency.
Inquiries of the Ministry
On the orders of the day:

Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Prime Minister in the absence of the Secretary of State for External Affairs. In view of the fact, as reported in the Globe and Mail this morning, that the government of Indonesia has dropped armed paratroopers in Malaysia and that the government of Malaysia is sending a complaint to the security council of the United Nations, would the government now give consideration to cutting off aid to Dr. Sukarno?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as the Secretary of State for External Affairs has said, this matter is now under consideration; but, as it has also been pointed out, the only aid going to Indonesia this year is I believe a few hundred thousand dollars worth of wheat and flour.

A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Would the Prime Minister not agree that even though the aid is only in the form of wheat to the value of several hundred thousand dollars, this enables the Indonesian government to save foreign exchange and thus buy arms abroad?

Inquiries of the Ministry AGRICULTURE

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Agriculture. I wonder if the minister could say that such capital grants for construction would be extended until perhaps the 1967 centennial, giving these fairs a greater opportunity for adjustment?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harry W. Hays (Minister of Agriculture):
maintopic: CAPITAL CONSTRUCTION GRANTS TO A AND B CLASS FAIRS

maintopic: CAPITAL CONSTRUCTION GRANTS TO A AND B CLASS FAIRS
speechtext: I should like to ask a supplementary question. In the Brome-Missisquoi area this week end we are having a fair. Would the minister come to that fair and tell the dairy farmers what he told us in the house in respect of the dairy industry?

maintopic: CAPITAL CONSTRUCTION GRANTS TO A AND B CLASS FAIRS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if I have the time and I receive an invitation I should be very glad to go with the hon. member.

maintopic: PAYMENT OF SUBSIDY ON GRAIN TRANSPORTED BY FARMERS

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: PAYMENT OF SUBSIDY ON GRAIN TRANSPORTED BY FARMERS
speechtext:
On September 1, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot (Mr. Ri-card) asked me whether a farmer doing his own transporting by truck would benefit from the transportation subsidies.
The answer is yes. According to the regulations coming into force next September 14, a farmer will be able, from now on, to use his own truck to get his supply of feed grain, and that assistance will be granted to him at any mill in the area where his farm is located.
Under the present policy, he could not obtain any additional help when using his own truck for that kind of transportation.

Hon. Theogene Ricard (St. Hyacinthe-
Bagot): Mr. Speaker, could the minister tell the house whether the miller who provides his own means of transportation is also entitled to those subsidies?

maintopic: PAYMENT OF SUBSIDY ON GRAIN TRANSPORTED BY FARMERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I shall inquire about this, but I believe the answer will be yes.

maintopic: PAYMENT OF SUBSIDY ON GRAIN TRANSPORTED BY FARMERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to put a supplementary question. Must the farmer apply to the federal government in order to get this subsidy? Will the federal government pay this subsidy to the transportation company, which will then remit it to the farmer?

maintopic: PAYMENT OF SUBSIDY ON GRAIN TRANSPORTED BY FARMERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not think there is any difference in the cases just mentioned by the hon. member. The subsidy is always paid to the mill. Therefore, the miller will have to see to it that the farmer gets the amount to which he is entitled.

maintopic: PAYMENT OF SUBSIDY ON GRAIN TRANSPORTED BY FARMERS
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. In the event the miller would not give the farmer the money owing to him, will the federal government be able to step in so that the miller will hand over to the farmer the money to which he is entitled?

maintopic: PAYMENT OF SUBSIDY ON GRAIN TRANSPORTED BY FARMERS
speechtext: Order. This question should be placed on the order paper.

maintopic: PAYMENT OF SUBSIDY ON GRAIN TRANSPORTED BY FARMERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, with reference to the question asked by the hon. member for Nicolet-Yamaska a moment ago concerning the remedy which would be available to the federal government should a miller refuse to pay back an amount of money to a farmer, I wish to draw the attention of the house to the fact that, for nearly a year now, I have been raising questions which are somewhat related to that matter. In my opinion, too many privileges are granted agents selling feed grain and I think the minister should tell us what would happen if the federal government had no remedy at law to force them to reimburse such amounts to farmers.

maintopic: PAYMENT OF SUBSIDY ON GRAIN TRANSPORTED BY FARMERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as this is a legal question, I would like to inquire about it before giving an answer.

maintopic: PAYMENT OF SUBSIDY ON GRAIN TRANSPORTED BY FARMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Forestry.
Does the minister intend to issue a pamphlet on the procedure to be followed by a farmer to obtain a subsidy for the feed grain he moves himself?

maintopic: PAYMENT OF SUBSIDY ON GRAIN TRANSPORTED BY FARMERS
speechtext: Yes, we intend to do that, Mr. Speaker. We will send a pamphlet to all farmers who benefit or might benefit from that new policy.

maintopic: PAYMENT OF SUBSIDY ON GRAIN TRANSPORTED BY FARMERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question for the minister. Will such action be taken immediately or within a few months?

maintopic: PAYMENT OF SUBSIDY ON GRAIN TRANSPORTED BY FARMERS
speechtext: The new regulation comes into force on September 14. The publicity we intend to carry out in this connection will start immediately and the pamphlet to make farmers aware of the benefits of the new policy will be distributed as soon as possible.

subtopic: REPORTED DANGER TO QUEEN IN QUEBEC

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: REPORTED DANGER TO QUEEN IN QUEBEC
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the question I am about to put I ask with great diffidence, but it is one that I think has to be asked and requires an answer from the Prime Minister. My question is related to the visit of Her Majesty the Queen to Canada. In view of the threats of violence that have been made, the advertisements appearing in newspapers with particulars regarding opposition to the forthcoming visit in respect of which demonstrations are planned, and so on, is the Prime Minister in a position to advise, not particularly what means are being taken to provide necessary precautions, but whether he agrees with the suggestion by the special committee for the royal visit that special precautions are not necessary; or is that not representative of the viewpoint of the government?

speakeroldname: Righi Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: REPORTED DANGER TO QUEEN IN QUEBEC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I can only say in respect of that visit that adequate security precautions are being taken, and every effort will be made to provide necessary precautions for the security and comfort of Her Majesty.
Perhaps I might also be permitted to express my own feeling that it does not help
Inquiries of the Ministry very much in this respect when exaggeration and extreme publicity are given to the violent statements made by those who are speaking only for themselves and, in one case at least, by a person who has spent the previous 12 months in jail. I cannot think, Mr. Speaker, that it adds anything to the effectiveness of security to have that kind of statement given such exaggerated publicity.

subtopic: REPORTED DANGER TO QUEEN IN QUEBEC
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister has expressed himself in a way that I think will receive general support, though always subject to the one qualification that we must be very careful not to restrict freedom within appropriate limits. However, I do point out to him the fact that, according to the Gazette of Wednesday, petitions are being secured by an organization known as rassemblement pour l'independance nationale, and advertisements are appearing in one Montreal daily newspaper in respect of plans for meetings to protest against the visit, and for demonstrations, which were freely admitted in detail on the telephone yesterday by a feminine voice answering the number which appeared in the newspaper advertisement. Would the Prime Minister have this situation looked into?

subtopic: REPORTED DANGER TO QUEEN IN QUEBEC
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Speaker, I will do that.
