The house resumed, from Wednesday, September 2, consideration of the motion of Mr. Pearson:
That the government be authorized to take such steps as may be necessary to establish officially as the flag of Canada a flag embodying the emblem proclaimed by His Majesty King George V on November 21, 1921-three maple leaves conjoined on one stem-in the colours red and white then designated for Canada, the red leaves occupying a field of white between vertical sections of blue on the edges of the flag.
And the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Diefenbaker, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Churchill.

Mr. Speaker, when the house adjourned last night I was speaking about the great contributions that had been made by various countries, particularly the Scandinavian countries, to both England and France. The Normans brought with them to England their culture, which was a Latin culture, and the Roman influence. William the Conqueror in some cases pursued a scorched earth policy but he brought order and set up a country that was never again invaded successfully by any other nation.
I also went on to point out that the Norman language enriched the language of the English. It became the language of the court, it became the language of the gentry, it became the language of the politicians, and Latin became the language of the church; while the poorer classes, the agricultural classes and serfs, used English. It was the melding of these two languages that made the English language as we know it today; a language whose origins are part French and part English, a language which is world wide, a language which is used by our neighbour to the south, the most powerful nation in the world. The melding of these strains gave rise to the tongue in which the plays of Shakespeare were written, in which Milton's "Paradise Lost" was written and in which Bunyan's "Pilgrim's Progress" was penned. It produced not only a great language, but unity; unity in a nation which controlled

the seven seas, which held sway over all the oceans of the world and which for years was the greatest peacemaker of all, as well as the greatest colonial organizer in the world.
It is also interesting to note, as I mentioned earlier, that the language of this nation became the language of the great country to the south. There was doubt whether it would be German rather than English, at one point, but George Washington gave the deciding vote in favour of English.
Thus it was that this great British nation came into conflict with the French in New France. Let me remind hon. members that the population in New France at the time of the battle of Quebec was just around 50,000 people. They were people who were heavily taxed and badly looked after, grumbled at by King Louis of France whenever they asked for help. Historians say he would like to have written off the colony and forgotten it. The officials were rapacious. They taxed the colonists whenever they could, stayed long enough to make fortunes, then returned to France to live on their illgotten gains. Certainly there were good officials, but the bad ones overshadowed them.
Is it any wonder, then, that these colonists, given the benefit of free trade under the British constitution and freedom from taxation on their goods as well as freedom of religion and the opportunity to retain the French language and the French code of civil law, were glad to accept these things? To an oppressed, heavily taxed people, robbed by some of their intendents, this represented a freedom they had never enjoyed.
What was the attitude of the English themselves? They were on most cordial terms with the French. We are told they laboured in the fields side by side with these sons of France and worked together with them on other jobs as well. We read that during their second winter in Quebec the English collected five hundred pounds sterling to help the French. This is a sum which would be worth well over $30,000 in terms of today's money. The garrison of Quebec gave one day's ration per month.
This was a friendship the colonists had not known from France. This was a freedom they had not known before. As a matter of fact, we learn that 3,000 Scottish soldiers who settled in New France liked the French girls so much that they married them. Here we see the introduction of some 3,000 young Scotsmen into the mainstream of the life of this colony. It meant, too, that 3,000 girls of
Canadian Flag
French origin were taken out of the marriage market. Talk about unity, what unity is there to beat that? Today, some people talk about disunity. What is wrong with history teaching in Canada if there is disunity? What is wrong with the politicians if there is disunity?
I want to say that the French appreciated the Quebec Act. They appreciated the treatment I have described here so well that when the American revolution came they stood side by side with their English compatriots and with the Indians and, with the help of the British navy and British soldiers, they defended this country successfully during the American revolution and during the war of 1812. This is unity. Who today tries to cause disunity?
The French and the English together made progress over the years. First there was Upper and Lower Canada. Then there was the province of Canada. Then we had confederation. Not 50 years after that the French and the English were found joining together to go to war when over 600,000 boys-yes and for the first time some women, too,-went abroad to defend freedom in the great struggle of 1914-1918. Some of them, both English and French, went to the help of their mother countries, and over 100,000 suffered casualties. But out of the ashes of that war came the treaty of Westminster. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that this was a move made by Sir Robert Borden when he insisted on signing the treaty of Versailles, confirmed in 1932 by a Conservative government under R. B. Bennett.
I come now to the second world war of 1939-45. Here again the English and French fought side by side to defend their mother countries, England and to an even greater extent France, against the invasion of Hitler. A great many of these boys and girls of Canada, principally the young men, lie buried in the fields of France, and on one of these graves- I have not seen it-is an inscription of particular significance. A gentleman from Vancouver wrote to me that there is a monument to an unknown soldier on the Normandy beachhead with the following inscription on the stone: "The sons of William the Conquerer come back to claim his land".
I ask you, Mr. Speaker, what greater unity could we have? Who is dividing this country today?
We have before us one of the most divisive issues which could be presented to parliament. Here in Canada we have a people whose stock is 44 per cent British, 30 per cent French and 23 per cent of other European

Canadian Flag
origin. The Prime Minister has made use of two issues which, in my opinion, are most divisive. The commission on biculturalism and bilingualism was appointed to go across this country and, as far as I can see, it has only stirred up trouble. Now the right hon. gentleman has brought in a flag of his own choice.
I do not want to be critical of the Prime Minister, because we all make mistakes. Where is the man who has not make a mistake? I sympathize with him, Mr. Speaker, but I say this was simply a tragedy; this was the thing to disunite the people, not to unite them. Nothing the Prime Minister could have done could have caused more trouble; no way he could have gone about it could have caused more trouble. Then we ask ourselves, why did he do it? It has been said that it was an election promise. If it was an election promise three Toronto daily newspapers did not know anything about it, because they did not carry a single line about it in their advertisements. Not one newspaper mentioned it.
On Friday, May 15 the Prime Minister said "Well, we have 37 important measures to come before the house". But the flag was not included in them. On June 3, though, he announced that he had cut this to 18 items, and the flag made its appearance. Why? Did he have a mandate from the people? This is a Prime Minister with a minority government. I ask hon. members on the other side of the chamber, did he have a mandate? How could he have a mandate, when he had a minority government and only 42 per cent of the vote? It has now been shown, according to the newspaper reports, that nine provinces are against the Prime Minister's personal flag and only one province is for it. But, Mr. Speaker, I have had letters from the province of Quebec as well as designs.
Here is where I think the Prime Minister is making a fatal mistake in coming to the conclusion that the people of the province Of Quebec want the flag he is personally proposing. I do not believe this is so, because not one of the designs I received nor one of the letters-and I received a goodly number-called for this flag. After speaking in this house previously I received several letters, most of them congratulatory. Even though they differed, and these people said they wanted a new flag, in my opinion the great majority of people in Canada are not in favour of the design proposed by the Prime Minister. This is my personal opinion, Mr. Speaker.

I say let us have a proper flag; let us have a flag that will be respected and accepted from the Atlantic to the Pacific. The dominion-provincial conference has been held in Charlottetown during the past few days. The other evening in the quietness of my office I thought what a wonderful thing it would have been if the Prime Minister of this country had presented the flag question to that meeting and had said, "You are going to change things. You are going to change the constitution. Let us get together now and work out the flag over the next two or three years", before 1967. Mr. Speaker, let us have a flag that every premier and the people in the provinces from the Atlantic to the Pacific will accept. Would it not have been a great thing if this had been done?
Hear, hear.

I do not think any members on the government side can disagree with that in their hearts and souls. I do not believe there is one hon. member opposite who would say this was not the proper course.
Now we are faced with this problem. The Prime Minister has introduced his personal flag. I say again that I have nothing against the Prime Minister in any way. I know it is a heavy load that any prime minister carries. However, contrary to all the rules of diplomacy he introduced his own flag. Did he consult the Leader of the Opposition or any of the other groups before he brought in this design? Not at all; he brought in his own flag.
In doing so, Mr. Speaker, there was no reference to the people at all, and no plebiscite. At the beginning the Prime Minister said there would not be a free vote; in other words, "If you do not vote for it you can go to the people". I say to you, Mr. Speaker, how in the world could the Prime Minister have gone about it in a more arrogant fashion than this?
Things have changed now, because nine out of ten provinces do not want a change or they want some other design. Le Devoir was very sympathetic last spring to the Prime Minister's flag; they were prepared to go along with him. Now the conclusion they have reached, as I gather from reading the articles that have appeared in this newspaper, is that they are fed up with the bumbling in connection with this issue; they do not want to go along with it any more. That is a very influential newspaper in the province of Quebec. They say "In May your ideas might not have been too bad, but in August your bumbling is too much".

I have stated that the correspondence and designs I have received in connection with the flag have led me to believe that the people of the province of Quebec have far better flags, far more acceptable flags which have been designed by the people of that province. Their designs are far more acceptable than that introduced by the Prime Minister. I feel rather sorry for the Prime Minister, Mr. Speaker, because his charted course has floundered. Now he offers summit meetings and a free vote, but this is all too late. Perhaps this is his only way out. I want to place on the record an article which appeared in the Cape Breton Post. This is very apropos:
Conservative M.P.'s are taking the right course on the flag issue, in stepping up their campaign in the House of Commons to persuade the government to refer the issue to a special parliamentary committee.
The issue should have gone to a parliamentary committee in the first place, but it's not too late for this to be done as a means of breaking the deadlock on the flag debate.
The Conservative tactics became evident Tuesday as the house plodded through the 14th sitting day of debate on the maple leaf flag resolution. Conservative after Conservative rose to press the point that a small all-party committee would cool off the steaming debate.
The Conservative proposition is that a committee should be empowered to recommend a flag and have it approved by the house. If the committee failed to agree unanimously on a flag, the issue should be taken to the people in a national plebiscite.
The prospect of a committee representing all groups in the Commons, arriving at an unanimous agreement on the flag does seem dim, but obviously such a committee should be the next step toward settling the issue.
The next step thereafter quite conceivably would be or should be a national plebiscite, which previously was recommended by this newspaper as the sure way of the country reaching a firm decision on the design of Canada's new flag.
All parties, including the Conservative party, appear to be agreed that a new flag is essential. It would be misleading to suppose that the Conservatives oppose the adoption of a new flag. The controversy on the issue revolves around a question of design.
I have said previously that the Prime Minister has my sympathy, because he is in about the worst mess possible. He said we cannot have a plebiscite on this issue. Why in the world can we not have a plebiscite? He has only to consider the action taken by previous Liberal leaders, who held plebiscites on issues that were just as emotional as this one; that were just as heart searching. I say to the Prime Minister that it is not too late for him to change his course. I suggest, in the interests of very important legislation that is waiting to be dealt with,
Canadian Flag
that he get on with the job and get this work done. I had a newspaper clipping from the Daily Packet and Times which said "The reason he is not getting on with it is that he has not the legislation prepared".
Mr. Speaker, if that is true we should adjourn this house and allow the members to go home, and the ministers should get together and prepare legislation. Why should the Prime Minister keep everyone here when he has nothing for us to do? I suggest the problem is one for the government to solve, not for the opposition to solve. I say with all seriousness as a Canadian that it is my desire to have the flag issue settled in such a way that our national unity will continue in the spirit which existed following the capture of Quebec, as evidenced by the intermarriage and the intermingling of the two races on a firm footing. These two peoples lived in complete unity of purpose and have defended this country over the years. They were faced with a war within a short period of our historic union, and won.
Mr. Speaker, in the interests of preserving that great unity I suggest to the Prime Minister that he allow a committee to commence its deliberations in respect of the flag issue. Let us adjourn this house until that committee has found a solution, or until the government has prepared other legislation. Over and over again it has been proved that the government does not now have legislation ready. Mr. Speaker, I think we can resolve the present difficulties with which we are faced. Whenever people get into trouble I always remember that poem which states:
One ship drives east and another drives west By the self-same winds that blow,
'Tis the set of the sails and not the gales Which determines the way we go.
Thank you, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, I am one of those members who have been somewhat reluctant to participate in this debate. I consider this to be one of the greatest debates this house has had for many years, and perhaps we will not have another as great for some years. I am not apologetic in any way for rising to contribute in my small way those words I feel are essential at this time. Despite the fact that government members, and perhaps some members of the opposition, have not contributed to it, I think in years to come students will regard this debate as part of the history of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, I have been reluctant to speak because I felt, as perhaps the Prime Minister

Canadian Flag
did, that a new flag might be essential to the unity of this country. I still feel that there is a possible solution to our problem, and I am not prepared to accept the idea advanced by those individuals who are ready to separate from the rest of Canada. I am not ready to accept the idea that a part of Canada, which I believe is part of my nation, should become a separate entity. I think those individuals who feel that part of Quebec, or Quebec itself, should separate from the rest of Canada are wrong, and I will do everything in my power to protect and defend my country, of which I believe Quebec is a part.
Mr. Speaker, I am not happy about what is happening in the province of Quebec, but I do not believe that those people in Quebec, who are deeply disturbed by the present situation, wish to be embroiled in this question. I have hesitated to take part in this debate because I am neither of Anglo-Saxon nor French Canadian origin. My father came from Poland and, although my mother was born in Canada, her parents were of Ukrainian origin. I often refer to myself in a jocular way as a half-breed, but at the same time I feel very strongly that I am a Canadian.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, I heard someone on the opposite side say "Hear, hear." I am very puzzled, and have been puzzled over the years, because of a question asked during the taking of the census. Most people in this country wish to be labelled and considered as Canadians.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, again I hear a member say "Hear, hear". We all want to be remembered as Canadians. I should like to remind those members on the opposite side that there is another problem inherent in that problem we are now discussing. We must decide whether we wish to be Canadians, or to be Polish Canadians, Ukrainian Canadians, Yugoslav Canadians, or Canadians of many other ethnic origins.
Or French Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, behind the main problem there is another problem which is difficult to isolate. I want to co-operate with all Canadians, but I expect in turn that they will co-operate with me. I should like to know why, during a census taking, some Canadians were labelled as French Canadians, for example. If an individual wishes to be identified as something other than just a

Canadian I would agree to that designation, but I should like to know why those of us who wish to be Canadians must disclose our racial background.
Mr. Speaker, I am sure my leader is aware of my position. I felt perhaps the establishment of a distinctive Canadian flag would lend itself to national unity.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext: Would not this distinctive flag help?

I do not know what distinctive flag would help create national unity, but I am sure that the flag your government has proposed is not accomplishing that which you intended.
Mr. Speaker, I have been very reluctant until this stage of the debate to say anything, because I honestly felt that perhaps at some time during this great debate something would be suggested that would be accepted by all parties. Unfortunately no suggestion has been put forward which is acceptable to all parties. There have been many suggestions put forward by the official opposition, and only by the official opposition, but none has been mutually acceptable. If this proposed flag is not mutually acceptable in this House of Commons, how could it possibly be mutually acceptable throughout Canada? I suggest to those members who have been pressing this flag issue that they should take stock of the situation at this stage.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to point out that we in the opposition are not debating this flag issue because we love to stay here all summer. Do not think for one moment that we are not jeopardizing our own position if we are taking the wrong course, but think what you are going to do to Canada. As I said, I have been very reluctant to participate in this debate because I was perhaps not convinced as readily as some. I too felt that there might have been some in between measure we could take. I still believe that today. But there is only one group that can do something about the matter, and that is the government. We are not the ones who are responsible for taking action in the House of Commons; it is the government.
The leaders of all parties are meeting. The debate going on in the House of Commons is the frontispiece, if you like. Behind it are the discussions that are being held between the Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition, the past leader of the Social Credit party, the leader of the New Democratic party and the leader of the Creditistes. I have referred to the past leader of the Social Credit party for

the simple reason that he is stumbling over himself in his hurry to get over to the other side of the house and have them accept him. Let us not fool around about that.
We have been told that this debate is a filibuster, but so many strange statements have been made by the past leader of that party that it is disgusting. In fact he has reached the point that he does not even know whether he wants the Social Credit nomination in his own riding. He wants the Liberal nomination. We might as well accept that fact, and the people of Canada might as well know it.
I am one of those who believe that a two party system is the most effective parliamentary system that can be devised. I do not believe for one moment that a third party is necessary, nor do I believe that you add to the effectiveness of the system by adopting another name. You simply have a special label and that is all. However, I am sure the Liberal party of today can accept many of the ideas and ideologies expressed by the Creditiste group, the Social Credit group or the New Democratic group, and I am sure that many of us in the Conservative group are also quite prepared to accept many of their ideas. We have done this in the past. This has nothing to do with the issue today.
Is your leader ready to do so?
Your leader is not ready.
The two members who sit behind me will substantiate that he was ready to accept them because some of their ideas represent ideas in which he believes.
On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, there is a subamendment before the house. Should we not be speaking to the subamendment?
I am sure what I am suggesting is unity. I am suggesting that the past Social Credit leader should unite with the Liberal party. That is exactly where he is headed.
Order. Perhaps the hon. member could direct himself to the subamendment.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure you will agree with me that what we want in this country is unity, and there cannot be unity if we are going to divide ourselves in the House of Commons in such a way that the people of the country do not know where they are being led. How can the country be led by minority groups, large or small; and if 20220-482
Canadian Flag
the leader of one of those groups is going to deviate where is the country headed?
I want to turn again to the subamendment.
Hear, hear.

Again I say that if at this moment the leader of the Social Credit group were to suggest that he was going to walk across to the government side, they would accept him and members on that side would not even interrupt me. The point is that we in Canada are going through a quiet struggle, a struggle that it is difficult for people to understand. It is difficult for me as a private member to understand. I should like to see the man who can show us the answer to this dilemma. I should like to see that man, because I do not believe the past leader of the Social Credit party is the man who will show us how it is to be done. There are those who want to call themselves French Canadians. We have no problem with them, but they have a problem within themselves.
You have a problem over there.
That is true. We have a problem.
Like the Ukrainians in Europe.

I say that I do not want to be labelled as a Ukrainian, nor do I want to be labelled as a Pole. I want to be labelled as a Canadian. I do not know the constituency of the hon. member who interjected, but if somebody will remind me of it I will put It on record.
It is a good French name.

The point is that I want to be a Canadian, and the sooner all of us want to be Canadians the sooner we will get to the root of the problem. Why do you want to be called French Canadians when it comes to the census but want to be labelled as Canadians when it comes to a flag? I ask that question. On the one hand you want to be labelled as a separate French Canadian group, and on the other hand you want to be labelled as Canadians.
May I say I have some very good friends among the French speaking members. I am looking at the Minister without Portfolio. I am sure he will agree that I have discussed with him the question of how we could get at the root of the problem.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext:
By a Canadian flag.

Canadian Flag

Why do they want special consideration on the one hand, and on the other hand do not want to be recognized as a separate group? Why do we want two flags? What are we supposed to ask for in this debate? I am asking today, what do we want? What does the government want? After we finish this debate what will we be in the midst of then? We will be in the midst of another debate which will be a contradiction of what the government are trying to do today. They are going to say to us that the union jack is all right in certain cases. What hypocrisy. You do not believe it. Why do you try to shove it down the throats of Canadians? I do not know what is behind the whole thing, and personally I do not think the Liberal party is behind this flag proposal. I do not think the cabinet is behind it. The only one who is behind it is the Prime Minister. This is the problem. I have a quotation here from Shakespeare.
Read it.

Sure I will read it. It might be a lot easier to take than my words: I refer to Julius Caesar, act one, scene two:
Caesar. Let me have men about me that are fat; Sleek-headed men and such as sleep o'nights. Yon Cassius has a lean and hungry look; He thinks too much; such men are dangerous.
Antony. Fear him not, Caesar, he's not dangerous: He is a noble Roman, and well given,
Caesar. Would he were fatter! But I fear him not; Yet if my name were liable to fear,
I do not know the man I should avoid So soon as that spare Cassius. He reads much; He is a great observer, and he looks Quite through the deeds of men; he loves no plays,
As thou dost, Antony; he hears no music; Seldom he smiles, and smiles in such a sort As if he mock'd himself, and scorn'd his spirit That could be moved to smile at any thing.
Such men as he be never at heart's ease Whiles they behold a greater than themselves-
I am suggesting at the moment, Mr. Speaker, that this is what the Prime Minister and the Prime Minister alone has done. He has thought to himself, for what am I going to be remembered. He said to himself well, the Leader of the Opposition was prime minister and he is going to be remembered for the bill of rights. For what am I to be remembered? He said, I am going to be remembered for the flag. He talked to a few of his colleagues in the cabinet. I stand to be corrected on this, but I understand it was suggested at one time that there were only a few, select members of his cabinet who were going to choose a design for the flag.
Well, be corrected, then. [Mr. Benldlckson.l
I suggested that I wanted to be fair about this.
Who told you that?

I read it In the Liberal press. I am suggesting that this country is being divided, and it is being divided not by the Liberal party, not by the Liberal cabinet, not by anybody except one man. This one man wants to immortalize the name of Pearson. He wants-

Order, please. May I recall to the hon. member that we are discussing how to conduct a plebiscite and what we should do with the results, whether they should be published in one way or the other. This is really the subamendment.
I should like to bow to your wishes, Mr. Speaker. I certainly do not want to divide-

I think all the members in the house must realize that a great deal of leniency has been given to the hon. member. I do not see where it is in order for an hon. member to indulge in a personal vendetta against any particular member, no matter what his official position may be. We are discussing the subamendment and under the heading "national unity" there is wide scope.

I am suggesting that a division is being created in this country, and it is being created by only one individual. I do not know how to skirt around this problem without referring to the particular individual. If I may refer to him as an hon. member, then I will do that. I do believe I am discussing unity at this particular moment. I do not want to deviate from your ruling, Mr. Speaker, or anything of the sort. However, I do want to be able to discuss unity. I have already suggested it is not the Liberal party that is dividing this country. I have suggested it is not the cabinet that is dividing this country. I am suggesting that-
Order.

I am suggesting that we can find unity only by avoiding one man's ambitions. This man is ambitious. I am suggesting to the members of the government and to government supporters that this man is dangerous to you. You are going to lose your seats because of this man's attitude.
Order.

Well, if it is all right for the Minister of Trade and Commerce to suggest it is dangerous for the Conservative party

to have a certain leader, I am sure it must be all right for me to make the same suggestion to the Liberals.
Where are we heading? I will tell you, Mr. Speaker, where we are heading. I have a letter here, and I do not mind telling hon. members that I did not receive very many letters concerning this problem. This is one of the reasons I have not participated in this debate heretofore. I have a letter here from which I am going to quote very briefly. This letter is from one of my constituents, a French Canadian if you want to use that hyphenated name. She is Mrs. Roland Bosse from Perigord, Saskatchewan, which is a French community. I receive a great reception when I go there. Let me tell the members of the government what they are doing.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext: Is the letter in French or English?

Let me tell the hon. member what she says about the flag:
I'm sending you three letters that I cut out from "The Western Producers, The Young Co-Ops' Page", and they express my feelings better than I can express them myself.
I am just going to quote this letter. I am sure she did not want to hurt my feelings, and I do not want to offend her in any way: Canada, O Canada
"United we stand; divided we fall." This is an old saying that historians often use in reference to the fall of a country. Does this hold true today? We are faced with the division of our country today, and most of us realize this. All over this large country of ours a team to study bilingualism and biculturalism has been set up, headed by Andre Laurendeau and Davidson Dunton. Exchange students are being sent to Quebec and vice-versa.
The new flag has raised the question of further split. I am sure all of us would be content with the old flag if the new one had to be brought in at the expense of a division in our country. If we all work for the interest of the country I am sure a division can be prevented.
Now, this expresses her sentiments, and I underline the fact that it expresses my sentiments. I do not want a division in this country. I believe that Quebec is part of Saskatchewan, if you want to look at it that way. I believe I have an interest in that province. I have tried my utmost to understand the situation. I believe that today the Prime Minister is going headlong into something, and he does not know where it is going to end. If he wants to immortalize his name he will do so in one way, and that will be as the man who divided this country.
This is not going to be a laughing matter when it happens. I do not regard this as something funny. My parents came to this 20220-482J
Canadian Flag
country because it had a future, and they would not want to see a division in this country. If you think it is a silly matter, then you do not respect the historical background of our flag. Let us not forget that right today Britain does not want to allow Southern Rhodesia its independence until such time as freedom and free speech for all its people are guaranteed within its confines. This is what that country stands for. This is what my people came to; this is what we want, and this is what I want. Do you not want it?
I heard overtures from the Social Credit party suggesting we should propose closure, and the hon. member who sits behind a former leader of the Social Credit group suggested he would be willing to impose closure. Is this what this new flag is going to represent-lack of freedom of speech? This is not what my people want; this is not what I want. I am sure this is not what government members want.
Speak for yourself.

I am speaking for myself and I hope I speak for a lot more people when I speak for freedom of speech. Is the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Deschatelets) suggesting for one moment that freedom of speech is not important?
I said speak for yourself.

In uttering those words at this moment he is expressing a freedom of speech that is unknown in many countries. In fact if he spoke them in some countries he would be taken behind the curtain, and it would be an iron curtain.
I am suggesting that there is nothing to prevent the government from taking action which will provide a solution for this problem. Obviously the opposition is not being foolhardy. We are doing this because of the type of letters we get, and because of the type of reaction across the country. Obviously we are speaking for a minority, if it is such; but it could be a majority, and I am suggesting the longer this debate is prolonged it will become a majority. I am sure most of the government supporters will agree with that- that it will be a majority, if it is not one already.
I know what the reaction was in the press gallery when this debate started. Members of the press gallery said public opinion would solidify itself behind the flag issue and that the Prime Minister would be all right. This is what they thought; but let me point out to the government members and the members of the press gallery, if it is not obvious to

Canadian Flag
them already, that public support has not solidified behind the government, has not backed up the Prime Minister in his bold, foolhardy venture. The man who is Prime Minister today had a bold and imaginative idea. It is all right to be bold and imaginative, but he is going to learn it is over his head and that it is about time he quit.
Why must he pursue this course? It is for the simple reason, as I said before, that he wants to immortalize himself through the flag. Why must the rest of his party be subjected to that type of treatment? I suggest to his party that the mixed caucus it holds stinks. This idea stinks and the Prime Minister should not go through with it. I suggest that his party should not pursue this course because it is foolhardy, because they are going over a cliff. Like lemmings they are heading for the sea. There are a lot of good members on the government side; perhaps some of the finest members are found on the other side, and I would like to see their faces again, but not in shame. If they divide this country it will not be for a day or a year or two; it will be for a long time.
I do not like to see my fellowmen fighting me. I do not like to fight my fellowmen. I see no reason. Because of what-a flag? I am sure a country can exist without a flag.
We are the only one.

If we want to preserve our unity, if we have any respect for each other we can exist without a flag. If this is what you say, then we have done it for over 100 years.
Speaking of history, at one stage when Lord Durham was preparing his report he had a sheaf of notes and he jotted down what came to his mind. The thought that entered his mind on one particular occasion was that this was a country without a history. This he jotted down, and later that day the maid entered his study to clean up and she saw these notes. I understand she was a French maid, and when she saw what he had written she thought it was wrong, and she wrote that on his notes.
May I ask the hon. member a question?

Just hold on a minute. When Lord Durham saw his notes in the morning he realized he had been wrong and that this woman knew what she was talking about. He asked her to explain why she had written on his notes, and she told him that Canada was rich in its history, even at that date.

We are not an emerging nation. We are not a nation that all of a sudden has got its independence. We are going to celebrate our 100th anniversary. We have a history. Are you to deny what has happened in the past? Am I to deny it? Stalin told his people, "Things happen this way." After him Khrushchev came along and said what happened under Stalin did not exist. Are those in Germany today, much as they dislike what happened in Germany, and much as a lot of us dislike it, to deny it happened? They cannot deny that they had a history. They had a history, much as we may dislike it.
Somebody said Wolfe fought Montcalm. Wolfe defeated Montcalm, somebody said; but the other point of view is that Montcalm surrendered to him. It does not matter how you look at it. The point is that this happened, and much as we may like or dislike certain events, they did happen; and much as the government supporters may dislike what is happening here today the fact is that there are those who want to preserve history as we know it, and I want to be associated with those people who want to be proud of our history.
I am amazed that the Prime Minister, a past history professor, should discard our history. What reason is there in this?
You know something about the Poles and the Ukrainians, don't you?

I know something about Canada, and that is what I am interested in. The point I am making is this-that the Prime Minister, a former history professor, says that history is to be forgotten and that we are going to start from scratch. And scratch it is. Somebody has suggested to me that if you draw three twigs on one base- a chicken's foot-that is the flag in winter. The Prime Minister is dividing this country today in such a way that I am ashamed. I have a letter here, but before I read it I should like to put on record a comment by Lubor J. Zink which I think sets out the situation very clearly.
All this sowing of nationalistic mistrust, which cannot but produce a harvest of hatred and strife is done by allegedly rational men motivated by visions of a strong united Canada.
I am sure that at one point the Prime Minister must have thought he was unifying Canada. I am equally sure that at this stage he is bound to realize he has not done so. He has divided us. I do not mind telling the supporters of the government that if there had been a free vote at an early stage

of this debate I might have felt as they do. But I have since changed my mind, as I think a great many Canadians have also changed their minds. I do not know whether I speak here for an ethnic group. I know I can speak as one member of an ethnic group. And I say the Prime Minister is wrong and that he had better consider the situation again.
We have offered alternatives. We have suggested a plebiscite. It is true that in a sense this was a negative proposition-
Your own member voted against it.

I do not care how he voted. That is the freedom he enjoys. There was no effort in this party to prevent a free vote. But there was no free vote on the government side.
We offered another alternative. It must be remembered that it was the Conservative opposition, and the Conservative opposition alone, which offered this other suggestion and I am proud to stand with it. No one on the government side put forward the suggestion we now offer that this question should now be placed before a committee. If hon. members opposite want to save the face of the Prime Minister they should plead with him to accept this proposal. I do not know how they will go about it. I have tried in a quiet way to suggest to private members that they should make such an approach but, apparently, they were unable to get through to him. For anyone to suggest, as did the leader of the Social Credit party, that this party is not consulted by its leader-I think the blame should be laid on the government side of the house-is absolutely disgusting.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member, but his time has expired.

Up to this point I have not taken part formally in this flag debate, but at the present time I feel we have reached a stage where there must be some alternative course to the one we are following now. Therefore, I wish to speak briefly in order to put forward a few suggestions which I think are vitally urgent as far as an alternative line of approach is concerned.
Many charges have been made by various members who have taken part in this debate, including the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Korchinski) who has just spoken. In my opinion, this is not an occasion for further remarks which might arouse emotions or feel-
Canadian Flag
ings. It is a time when we must realize it is imperative for us to reach some kind of agreement which can bring this spectacle, of which we are all a part, to an end.
I do not care for the way in which the flag issue was introduced into this house. I think the timing was poor. I think the method which was used to bring these resolutions before us can hardly be considered the best. Neither does the three maple leaf design appeal to me as far as its beauty is concerned, or in terms of the type of flag I should like to see this nation have. I must admit however that since the debate began I have learned much more about the history of the three maple leaf emblem and the extent to which it has been tied in with Canada's story from the beginning. But somehow it seems to lack the aesthetic appeal which a flag should have.
On the other hand, I have taken the stand for a number of years that Canada should have a distinctive Canadian flag. I have spent most of my adult years overseas living in foreign countries and it has been my privilege to share part of the general regard which, for the most part, nationals of foreign countries have for Canadians. I do not think this regard arises so much out of what has been done by our successive governments. Rather I think it has risen because of what Canadians have done. It seems that whether they are of English stock, or French stock, or whether they have another ethnic origin, Canadians are able to make friends with and influence effectively the people with whom they come into contact. This is one of the reasons I have for thinking that Canada has a definite role to play in a world whose affairs come closer to us each year.
One of the questions which has been asked of me over and over again in the course of years is: Why don't we have a flag which is distinctively Canadian? People in other countries often ask whether we still belong, as a colony, to Great Britain. They wonder whether or not we are an autonomous nation. They find our position difficult to understand. In June I was part of a delegation which visited Europe, and while there I talked to many of our people, who are doing a wonderful job-in fact, it seems to me they are better liked than they were ten years ago when they first went to Europe. But I did not find a single officer serving in Europe with our Canadian forces who did not voice the wish that we might have some distinctive flag expressive of the distinctive and unique role which Canada is playing at the present time. As to my own convictions with

Canadian Flag
regard to this, I have tried to respect the opinions of others. I do not think this is a matter we should use in order to develop animosity among ourselves. Goodness knows, we have little enough of a national purpose today without trying to break down further what there might be.
So, Mr. Speaker, I am of the opinion that we ought to try to come together in some non-partisan way in order to work out together a design that would be acceptable to all of us, in a way that the majority of Canadian people would agree with, and which would make them proud of the flag decided upon. I do not think it has been helpful to any of us in this house or to the nation to have this debate carry on as it has now for 20 days. I believe it is the responsibility of every one of us in this house to endeavour to make it possible to come to some mutually acceptable agreement, an agreement that is not forced upon one or the other and is not legislated upon one or the other.
I am confident that such an agreement is possible. I am sure that if we were to lay out the vehicle by which this coming together could be made possible, we would even surprise ourselves how quickly we could come to some agreement. I do not think there is anything to be gained by charging the Liberals at this time that they did not do this the right way, or because they did not consult on a non-partisan basis or did not adhere to their original position that there would be a free vote, as was said at the beginning. These things belong to the past. I do not agree with the tactics and the policy the Conservative opposition have used. I do not think this is the time to try to arouse feelings or to condemn them for that. I believe the time has come when we should try to come together in order to reach some agreement.
Mr. Speaker, I wonder whether the hon. member would permit a question?

If the hon. member does not mind, Mr. Speaker, I would be very pleased to answer his questions afterwards. I find that this flag debate has become odorous in the nostrils of our own countrymen, and a spectacle to other countries which must cause them to smile in a tolerant way, as though they were watching children quarrelling at play. We have become akin to high school cheering sections, tearing each other to pieces on the sidelines while the people who paid the price want us to get on with the game for which they paid.

It is time we got down to the serious business of running our country's affairs, which we have been sent here by the people to accomplish. We are in danger of not holding the country together at all so that any flag of any description can have anything to fly over. If we do not behave like responsible, mature people, we will not be doing anything more than reserving a picture of the map of Canada in a page of world history of something that once was-a faded camelot. You can colour it "shattered".
Unless there are ulterior motives on the part of some individuals-and I do not believe this is so in this house-reasonable men should be able to arrive at a reasonable and fair solution to our unnecessary dilemma. At the heart of our democratic process is the basic philosophy of majority rule with flexibility of action to make required concessions to a minority opinion. It has been said that politics is the art of the possible. There is nothing wrong with that. But I believe it is impossible for us to continue as we are going on at the present time. The only result that can come to pass by having the government resort to closure directed at those who are opposing the three maple leaf design, and to have them fail in their objective, would be to have it replaced by a more acceptable design.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I believe it is possible for us to come together. That is why I am speaking in this manner at this time. We can come together on this issue so that the House of Commons may proceed with the legislation that is vital to our country. I would suggest, first of all, that the Prime Minister call, immediately after Labour day, another meeting of the leaders. I would urge the Prime Minister to consider this request. Second, I suggest that a committee be set up to which both flag resolutions could be referred. It has been proposed that this committee comprise 15 members; I have no objection to that. But I do not think we should demand of this committee a degree of unanimity that it is impossible to expect if it is there as a requirement. I believe we should accept such a committee being set up; we should accept those who are suggested to represent the different parties on that committee in good faith, in that they will consider the resolutions and be able to come to some mutually acceptable agreement.
I am sure that if this committee were to be set up on that basis there could be achieved just as great a degree of unanimity as there was in the former committee in 1946.

Third, this committee should be given one month to deliberate to seek a mutually acceptable alternative. This would bring us past the date of the Queen's visit. If the committee could come to an agreement in less than 30 days, all to the good; then their report should come back to the house. The fourth point is that when the report comes back to the house, if it received mutual acceptance in the committee the following debate should be limited to the party leaders in connection with the recommendations of the committee. In the event that it was impossible to come to a mutually acceptable agreement in a month, then the matter should be referred again to a meeting of the leaders.
How long did the previous committee sit? I wonder, Mr. Speaker, whether the hon. member would consider that, in the light of his suggestion that the committee sit for one month.
The hon. member has asked how long the previous committee sat.
Yes, Mr. Speaker, in the light of the hon. member's suggestion of one month.

In answer to that question I would say that I do not think that length of time would be required at this point. We have had 20 days of debate up to this time. If we would be honest with each other and would admit our own feelings in regard to this debate, I believe it would be practically unanimous that most of us are fed up with the way this debate has been going on, and would like to see some alternative. As I talk to different members I seem to sense that there is a determination or desire to come together, rather than to let this matter continue as it has been.
If agreement could not be had in a matter of a month's deliberations, then the question could be referred back to the leaders again and if necessary some alternative action could be taken. As a further alternative, this question could again come back to the house. I believe these suggestions are reasonable, Mr. Speaker. I believe these suggestions are necessary because it troubles me to think how we can expect to continue this debate through the next weeks of September and be in any frame of mind ourselves or to have developed within our own country an attitude favourable to the visit of Her Majesty the Queen. Certainly what we are doing now is encouraging those elements within our society that resent her coining and would do violence to her. This is something that is in-
Canadian Flag
tolerable, and certainly not in keeping with the reputation, dignity and loyalty that Canadians and Canada have portrayed as far as the crown is concerned.
Mr. Speaker, if this suggestion in respect of setting a time for a leaders meeting can be acted upon by the Prime Minister before we go home for the Labour day week end, it would give us all time to reflect seriously on the situation that now exists and to probably sense in a more realistic way the attitude of the people in this country. Then perhaps we can go along with the spirit that should have developed as a result of the first centennial celebrations which have just concluded in Prince Edward Island. If we find it is not possible to do that, then we are left open to the kind of criticism that is mounting from every side, criticism from those Canadians who are loyal to what Canada is and who have ambitions and desires for the continuation and projection of what Canada should be in the future.
Typical of this criticism is that editorial which appeared in the Montreal Gazette of yesterday entitled "If the Fathers Came Back". At this recent celebration in Prince Edward Island certain men portrayed the fathers of confederation and acted out the events that took place 100 years ago. If those men, who re-enacted those scenes, had actually been the Fathers of Confederation back in our midst, what would they have thought about what they found here in Canada?
The part of this editorial that impressed me very much reads as follows:
But saddest of all for the fathers would be their look at what takes place today In the capital city on the shore of the Ottawa river. Here was to be the parliament of the nation-a parliament with wisdom and skill and eloquence, capable of seeing and shaping a broadening destiny. Instead they would find a faded hope, a tawdry spirit, a pitiful wrangle, an exhibition of how little littleness can become.
The vision they had has departed. The parliament that heard the voice of Thomas D'Arcy McGee, and the good humoured good sense of Macdonald, and the blunt integrity of George Brown, and the fiery statesmanship of Cartier has become a gathering that has lost all faith in itself, that knows not what to do, that lets the sun come down on day after day of drab uselessness.
I do not believe that anyone who is trying to follow the thoughts I am projecting has any purpose or useful intent in interjecting things that would be contrary to how the general public is coming to regard us and this institution. Summarizing my remarks as briefly as possible, I would urge the Prime Minister to reconvene the leaders meetings again on Tuesday after Labour day, and

Canadian Flag
suggest that the leaders, including the leader of the official opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), should seriously consider and display a willingness to let a committee have one month to attempt to work out a solution to this problem. Again I say I am convinced that if 15 men, even if some were those who have expressed themselves very strongly on both sides of this matter, could come together on this basis, before 30 days had passed-and perhaps even before one week-they could come to a decision which would be mutually agreeable to at least the vast majority of the party representatives, if not a unanimous decision. Who knows but what this thing could be resolved even before the Queen came here, by our own free will and by our serious intent to resolve a problem today that has degenerated into a hopeless situation.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I would repeat this suggestion with the thought and, yes, may I say with the prayer, that we will all seriously consider this or some similar avenue of approach that would end this damaging and futile debate in which we are engaged at this present time. I think it is the responsibility of every one of us, who claim to be loyal Canadian citizens, to use our every effort and influence, on the basis of loyalty to the nation and with a sense of national purpose, to see that this thing does come to some such conclusion, which I am confident can come to pass.
Thank you.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I ask the hon. member a question? Yes, Mr. Speaker, I am very willing to agree to such a suggestion and would propose it if necessary. In fact, I think that every member in this house should bring to his individual leader, and discuss it with others, the suggestion that we make this a non-partisan discussion so that we as members of this House of Commons can come to some agreement. that what I have suggested is a logical approach. I think we should get together in respect of every possible or plausible suggestion, to accomplish this purpose.
I say this as a Canadian, not as a westerner. I have lived away from Canada too long to take a provincial view. I believe that Quebec is my Canada, as much as Alberta is, and I should like to think that members from Quebec feel that way about other parts of Canada. speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. With regard to the point of order raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre, perhaps I should have tried to give a ruling earlier. However, as the hon. member knows, the Chair has tried to interpret the rules of relevancy as leniently as possible in this debate. While the hon. member for Red Deer was speaking it was my opinion that his remarks related to the aspect of unity stressed in the subamendment before the house, and that is why I did not think he should be called to order.

May I make one remark, Mr. Speaker. I forgot even to mention the subamendment. I did not consider that the previous speaker was referring to it at all. What I had in mind saying was this. I have been in favour of a plebiscite but I am not sure whether or not it could serve a useful purpose now. I do not think it should be connected with an election. I am even in favour of the subamendment because I think that is the way a plebiscite could be most effective. On the other hand, at this point I think we should be talking about the situation in which we find ourselves, because I believe that because of that situation we are going to have to find some other solution, even though earlier we would have liked to see a plebiscite held.

Will the hon. member permit another question? I was interested in his remarks that we should not expect unanimous agreement in this committee. In view of the statement made by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) that there should be a virtually unanimous view, would he not agree that such a committee would likely be very fruitless, having in mind the veto power granted in that way?

I was very careful to state and I reiterate now that I do not think you can legislate unanimity. It is like trying to bring a boy and girl together and telling them they must love each other. It does not work
Canadian Flag
out that way. But if we could come together with a sense of co-operation and good will, forget about the demand for unanimity, and set up an ordinary committee I believe we could achieve unanimity far more easily than if we attempted to legislate it. Let us forget the veto. Let us forget all of that. Let us not use such words. If we could not reach general agreement the matter could come back to the leaders, but I am confident that we could come to an agreement and even surprise ourselves.
Before the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Nugent) speaks, may I ask the hon. member for Red Deer another question?
Yes.
If I heard him correctly, he said he was in favour of a plebiscite. Yet the other day he voted against it. How does he explain that?

I did not vote against a plebiscite at all. I voted against a subamendment with a set of questions with which I did not agree. That is why I voted the way I did. I have advocated a plebiscite right from the beginning. In fact, I believe it was an hon. member of this party who suggested for the first time that the counting of the vote should not be done on a regional or provincial basis, but on a national basis. I think this would have been an excellent way of arriving at a solution to the problem, but I think that at the present time we have gone beyond that point. I believe the Liberal government would have been far better advised if they had adopted some such proposal at the beginning.
Then I can take it from the hon. member's remarks that he is in favour of the subamendment and the amendment before the house?
I said I was in favour of the subamendment proposed yesterday as it relates to a plebiscite.
And you are prepared to vote for it?
Don't put words in my mouth.
That is why we want you to explain yourself fully.

From the very beginning, long before the flag issue was brought before the house in the form of a resolution, I have talked plebiscite. However, I qualify my statement at the present time because I think that

Canadian Flag
as a result of the way in which the government introduced the matter and the way in which the debate has developed a plebiscite is not the answer to the problem now, although it is an approach that should have been taken before.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Retreat.
You will never vote against the Liberals.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure most members of the house were much impressed by the sincerity of the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Kor-chinski) in what I considered a great speech that he made this afternoon. I am glad there has been a little comedy relief since then, prior to my rising, because I thought his was a pretty tough act to follow.
With regard to the suggestions of the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson), the leader of the Social Credit party, I can agree with him on one point, that the matter should go to a committee. However, it did seem to me most significant and very peculiar that he should propose a time limit of one month for the committee and a limiting of the debate to the leaders afterward, if the committee should not be unanimous in its recommendation. Neither the hon. member for Red Deer nor anyone on the government side has ever bothered to explain the necessity for the rush. Why does this matter have to be concluded within a specified time or in such a hurry or at a non-stop pace? Surely those members who are so exercised about a new flag regard the matter as serious enough that the problem should be dealt with by the house in its own good time, so that everybody can be heard and every voice from across the country can be heard and considered.
If the hon. member for Red Deer was serious in the platitudinous speech he just made he should have at least explained the necessity for the rush. If he wants the matter to go to a committee, why does there have to be a time limit? Why is there any hurry at all to finish the flag debate? I cannot understand why the committee should be limited to 15 members. I am certain the house is aware that a previous parliamentary committee was able to deal with this matter and bring about a good deal of agreement. On that occasion there was no time limit and the committee finished its work within a reasonable length of time, and made a very reasonable suggestion which I think had general support in the house.

There is only one reason why we are having any trouble with the flag debate. It is the manner in which the government is handling the matter. I would think that anyone who had the temerity to make the suggestion that the hon. member made should deal with the aspect of time and tell us why there is a rush. What is wrong with the government's putting aside a very contentious issue and bringing forward more urgent legislation? What is wrong with putting this matter aside for a while and letting tempers cool and negotiations be conducted? What is the reason we have to have a change in our national flag right now?
I was very concerned this afternoon, when the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) a question, to see the reaction of some of the government supporters. They wanted no compromise line followed with regard to this affair. Surely the government should be aware by now that a majority of the people of Canada are not in favour of the three maple leaf design. I am willing to concede it may be possible that a majority of the people want a change in our present national flag, but since the government is insisting that only one flag be considered and since the opposition is aware that a majority of the people of Canada do not want that flag, we have one simple duty to perform, to make sure that the flag resolution does not pass.
There has been only one difficulty throughout the debate, one factor leading to dissension within the country. I refer to the method of handling the flag issue. After all the speeches that have been made and the numbers of letters and newspaper articles that have been quoted, surely the Prime Minister must be aware it is his method of handling the matter that is dividing the country. Once the error has been pointed out and has become so apparent, what is wrong with a man who will not change what is obviously a very bad plan? This, I think, must puzzle the minds of even the most loyal Liberal backbenchers. I would feel a little better about it if the Prime Minister had explained, or even any of the government supporters had explained, the urgency connected with the matter of the flag.
We have asked the question again and again, why the rush? No one has explained why the government is handling the matter in such a hurry. I am willing to listen to any member, and I hope some member over there will get up and explain why it has to be run through non-stop. There is only one explanation that comes to my mind. It is the Prime Minister's

reputation for retreat and somersault, and he is afraid to do anything now. Surely, with the kind of insistence there has been, with the kind of trouble there is in this country today, with the heavy demands that are being made on such a logical basis, this is the one time when the Prime Minister should reverse his stand and receive general credit across the country.
The last time I spoke in this debate, Mr. Speaker, I quoted only small portions from two letters because it distressed me to find this feeling of division in our country. It was distressing to find feelings of resentment against Quebec and therefore I quoted only briefly from these letters. After listening to the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Korchin-ski) I think perhaps I would have been wiser to have gone into that aspect in more detail. We certainly do not achieve unity in the country by closing our eyes to the feelings that people express. It may well be that a certain amount of the correspondence members receive comes from crackpots, intemperate or violent people, and this would have little or no effect upon a responsible member.
Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, that is not the case here. The volume of mail is too large and the tone of many of the letters indicates such a high degree of intelligence and responsibility that we must take very seriously these symptoms of the illness that affects this country today, since the Prime Minister started this method of trying to change our national flag. The Edmonton Journal is the only daily newspaper in northern Alberta and it covers the entire northern half of the province. I think it is a fairly responsible newspaper. The only time I do not feel it is responsible is when it is against me during election campaigns. Other than that, I am sure the publishers and editors try to do their job. On August 25, page 4, the entire top half of that page of the Edmonton Journal was taken up by an article and included a three-column cut of the Prime Minister. The heading is "The Brink of Disaster?".
Perhaps I will have to put the whole of this article on the record, not because I agree with it but because that feeling is so current that the only daily newspaper in northern Alberta gives it prominence. I feel, therefore, it is my duty to bring it to the attention of this house. This feeling of resentment, of puzzlement, was not evident in my area before this flag debate started. I will say that over the last year there has been an expression of puzzlement as to what exactly the members from Quebec want. What is this
Motions for Papers
new feeling of nationalism in that French Canadian province? This article is headed "Partition for Canada; it may be the only way says Edmonton's H. B. Turner." I do not know who Mr. Turner is. I may have met him some time, but I cannot place him at the moment. I quote:
I suggest that the blackmail Liberal government of Mr. L. B. Pearson has done more to dissolve confederation than any group could have done had it deliberately set out to accomplish this fact.
Now, that is just the first paragraph. There is the word "blackmail" there. I suggest that if there is this feeling, then part of the reason for it is that there has been no explanation in this house by this government for rushing this flag through. There has been no explanation of the method they are using and why they are using it. There has been silence from the government supporters. There has been a stubborn, steadfast refusal to handle this matter of the flag in the manner in which it was handled before, and there has been apparently a complete blindness and deafness to the situation in Canada today. The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson) had the effrontery to suggest we are always responsible for this house becoming disreputable; that this flag debate is bringing down the standard of the house. I suggest that when the government starts determinedly on a course to try to foist a flag on the country in this manner, when we know the majority of the people do not want that flag, when there is no alternative action, when they refuse to handle it in any manner other than by force, then we have no alternative but to do what we can to make sure that that course is not successful.
May I call it five o'clock, Mr. Speaker?
