Bill No. S-39, respecting Meota Pipe Lines Ltd.-Mr. Nugent.

The house resumed from Thursday, August 20, consideration of the motion of Mrs. Konantz for the second reading of Bill No. S-6, to incorporate the Bank of Western Canada, and the motion proposed thereto by Mr. Perron.

Mr. Speaker, I fully support the amendment moved the other day by the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Perron) to the effect that Bill No. S-6 should not be read a second time but deferred for six months. This would give the mover and all those who support the bill an opportunity to consider carefully the remarks made by the hon. member for Beauce. It would also permit them to study the merits of his statement, as well as the suggestions he made to the house in this connection.

I wish to point out at the outset that if I participate in the killing of this bill, it is not that I want to prevent anyone from earning a living but there is a principle involved.
No matter who had presented this bill in the house, I would still be opposed to its passing, because my constituents elected me to the house precisely to help change the monetary system which we have to put up with since the Bank of Canada relinquished its powers to chartered banks.
I would therefore feel remiss if I let this bill pass today without giving my views on the present banks and monetary system.
I must tell you that I am very surprised to note that those who urge the nationalization of almost everything that belongs to private industry hardly think of nationalizing the most important business, that on which all the others depend as well as the public: the chartered banks.
Nobody talks about nationalizing credit institutions, though individual economic activities in this nation depend on them in a proportion of over 90 per cent.
Everything should be nationalized, according to some, except the gear-wheels, or machinery, so to say, of all the trusts which are to be nationalized. The existing trusts are to be destroyed, except the parent organization.
This reasoning is quite as ridiculous as if, wanting to get rid of all bees, we wasted our time killing them, while continuing to feed the queen bee which is responsible for what we want to eradicate.
And worse still, Mr. Speaker, instead of destroying this plague at its very source, permission is sought to add others and quite as pernicious ones.
This comparison, which some may think silly, is the exact replica of what is happening in our economy.
At this time we have eight chartered banks which distribute and control the economic blood stream of this nation, that is the money. Is there any reason for pride in the achievements of those institutions so far? When looking at the results, can we really say that those banks have played their part?
The country is constantly getting into debt day after day, year after year; every organization or individual must face this problem.
Is the country in need of money? It loses no time in borrowing from chartered banks. When the provinces need money, they hurry to borrow money from chartered banks. The same applies to our municipalities and our school boards.

Is it normal, Mr. Speaker, for a government that could order the Bank of Canada to create the money required, that could borrow directly for that bank, to have to go to chartered banks owned by private individuals? It just does not make sense and yet, it is exactly what the government is doing at the present time.
At this point, I should like to ask the hon. member for St. Jean-Iberville-Napierville (Mr. Dupuis) what he would think of the suggestion I am about to make. I address myself to him because he is the last one who is willing to understand what we want to rectify, for the simple reason that he does not understand the present system.
What would he think if, at the end of the month, he gets close to $3,000, I were to ask him to hand me that money and then to come and borrow it from me. That is what the Bank of Canada is doing now. It gives its money to the chartered banks and the government borrows it from them with interest.
With all the power those chartered banks now have, is it any wonder that the Canadian government, no matter which party is in office, should be at the mercy of a few hundred people who do as they please with it because they are empowered to restrict or extend credit.
How is it that, in a time of peace, we should be forced to tighten our belts due to a lack of money, when, to produce weapons of destruction, we can immediately find the funds required? Are those people for whom we provide jobs in wartime not there in peacetime? Are the materials we use to build destruction machines not there in peacetime? Are all those natural resources we develop in wartime not there in peacetime also? How is it that we are unable to use all those energies and resources in peacetime to build, improve, enlarge? How is it that we are unable to employ those people to build, etc. in peacetime?
It is because in peacetime the actual credit based on production and consumption capacity is not related to bank credit. That is why it is abnormal that the credit of the country should be controlled by private institutions instead of by a social credit agency which would seek to facilitate credit in the areas where the need for it is the greatest.
Mr. Speaker, I feel that there are now enough parasites living at the expense of the Canadian people.
When one considers that the Canadian government or parliament is ready to allow a new agency to do like the other chartered banks, namely to live at the expense of the
Private Bills
people who pay to support them, one realizes that this government merely works for those parasites, as we call the finance people; one is glad to help killing this bill, because there are enough chartered banks now; we do not need more.

Mr. Speaker, as my colleague from Dorchester (Mr. Boutin) said, the question is not whether the bill should be talked out or whether it should be delayed or passed. In my opinion, there is no need at present for another bank which would be known under the "French Canadian" name western bank of Canada. I see on page 5 of the bill that the bank would also be allowed to use the name Ban-que de I'Ouest canadien. It still remains, however, that it is designated as the bank of western Canada on the first page of the bill. But that is only a minor detail.
Mr. Speaker, the sponsor of the bill claimed that the setting up of another chartered bank would provide more credit in Canada. That is untrue.
Over the past 60 years, there has been a centralization of more than 30 banks; their number has even been reduced to eight under the Bank of Canada Act. That being so, would the addition of two more banks be justified now?
Mr. Speaker, the number of banks is unimportant; it is what banks can do which counts. At present, I think the chartered banks are being called upon to restrict credit. If the government itself controlled its own credit and credit issues, we would not have to put up with the effects such restrictions have on the financial system which is itself inadequate.
I note among the shareholders or those asking that the company be incorporated, the names of the hon. member for Winnipeg South (Mrs. Konantz) and that of the former governor of the Bank of Canada, Mr. Coyne, who, as we all know, experienced certain difficulties in 1954 about his ideas on the Canadian economy and especially on credit restrictions, because he had been pointing out for a few years that Canadians were living beyond their means and that they should tighten their belts.
It is not a question of increasing or not the number of banks. We, Social Crediters, fear that these banks and not the government control the issuance of credit to the nation. We want a change in that regard.
Therefore, if we are restricted to a particular amount when the government claims to control credit, how can we believe that more banks will create more credit. If you

Private Bills
have eight pounds to divide between eight persons, everyone will get one pound, but it there are ten persons, each one will not get one pound. According to the government, nine or ten chartered banks will make more credit available, but this is precisely the proof that its monetary policy is unsound. "The more banks, the more credit". That is false. Normally, credit should be proportionate to the total production, to the potential output of the country, of its manpower, of its natural resources.
Private enterprise is not short of credit nowadays.
Mr. Speaker, the chartered banks are private financial institutions which should finance only the private sector in the Canadian economy. As a matter of fact, if I get credit from a bank, it is normal that it should charge interest. By lending me money, the bank does me a service and I must pay it interest, just as the worker is entitled to his salary. That applies in the private sector of the Canadian economy. However, there is no reason to increase the number of chartered banks which already exist because they can do the same thing, that is be of service to the population.
Besides, when you borrow money from a chartered bank, you must pay interest; that interest is included in the final price of the article sold. In that case, the bank's interest is covered. But here is where the present system fails. We lack the public financial institutions which could supply public credit, which is something entirely different. That is another sector of the economy which seems to be forgotten. It seems that no difference is made between private and public credit.
When I talk about a manufacturer, I talk about private credit. The same thing goes when I talk about credit granted to a farmer who harvests potatoes; that is private credit. As a matter of fact, the money he invests in his farm or machinery to grow potatoes is private credit.
But when I talk about bridges, highways, waterworks, viaducts, in short any public utility which serves everyone in general and no one in particular, everything should be financed in the same way the private sector is financed by private credit. Consequently, public utilities should be financed by public credit.
It does not make any more sense to finance public business from private funds than it would to finance private business from public funds. Today, we are taking advantage of the revenue of the private sector to fi-
[Mr. Langlols.l
nance sidewalks, waterworks, schools, streets, roads and bridges. The money needed for such public works comes from the private sector, nowhere else. In this connection, I think we could obtain the necessary credit, without interest and without having to go through chartered banks.
Instead of suggesting the establishment of a new chartered bank, which would be adding another one to the eight already existing, why not use the Bank of Canada in the various provinces of the country, with branches to finance public utilities? Then, chartered banks would only have to finance the private sector, which they would do very well.
My opinion as a mathematics professor is that the suggestion of establishing a new bank does not make any sense and is antimathematical. We will never swallow that kind of theory.
If it is nonsensical to use public credit to make investments in the private sector, it is even more nonsensical to inject private credit into the public sector to finance public business.
Bridges do not belong to me, roads do not belong to me as a member of parliament or as a private individual; they do not belong to me, even if they belong to everybody. If the Bank of Canada were to finance public business through its branches, we would pay much less interest for the construction of highways or bridges. Construction costs could be refunded at the depreciation rate of the public utility built or the natural resource developed.
If it is a bridge of $3 million, you would have a certain depreciation each year-engineers know what this depreciation would be. The amount is recovered each year. If the construction cost of the bridge were $3 million and the depreciation rate established at 5 per cent per annum, you would only have to recover the construction cost at a rate of 5 per cent per annum. That bridge would then be financed through public credit, without any interest. Thus we would not have to pay the cost of that bridge three times.
We know that as soon as the construction of a bridge is completed, it starts to depreciate. The bridge does not produce anything nor does it increase in value. Why should it be paid for three times? By using public credit, credit would be created and after completion the bridge would be paid for.
Mr. Speaker, I ask the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Dupuis) to pay attention to what I am saying. I ask him to listen care-

fully. He will soon see the ridiculous situation we are in now. He just has to establish the total value of our production to realize that we owe more than we actually have in value. I am referring here to the total debt of the country and to its total assets. We have more debts than accounts receivable. The same thing should be done for the United States, the richest country in the world. The United States, after having collected everything which was due to them, plus everything they owe, are still in debt.
In making these computations we unavoidably find that every country has a debt. How is it that every country has a debt when it has collected all its receivable accounts? To whom is it indebted? I would like the Minister without Portfolio to take the time to figure out where the shortcoming lies. He will then undoubtedly understand that there is something which is wrong in our financial system.
That is the reason why I believe we should make the changes. There is unavoidably hardship when our human laws come in conflict with the logical and natural needs of our citizens. Well then, it is illogical to create another chartered bank when there are already eight which are operating quite well and which can create all the private credit that the private sector needs. What is wrong is that the public sector must be financed by money from the private sector, and that results in a lack of credit in the private sector.
Why must the public sector repay sometimes four times the cost of construction? It is a little like the wheels of an automobile; the wheels of the private sector and those of the public sector are not turning at the same speed.
In fact, with a small wheel and a big wheel, we are apt to turn round in a circle. That is exactly what is being done today. One wheel is turning faster than the other. What we want is to balance the two wheels. At that time we shall go where we want and not where the wheels take us.
Mr. Speaker, as long as I am a member of this house, I shall oppose the setting up of another chartered bank. Perhaps I shall not object to a provincial bank. But, there again, we should know whether this bank would finance the private and the public sectors, because if its only object was to finance the private sector, I would oppose its creation.
Today, it is public financing which is lacking. It should be possible to finance public projects without having to pay the cost four or five times over; in other words, we shall
Private Bills
always have credit restrictions, and be unable to balance things, an inacceptable condition in a country like Canada, which should be the richest in the world, but where some people are still literally dying of malnutrition; all that can be attributed to our financial system as it is today.
Mr. Speaker, I object to this bill and I shall continue to do so.

Mr. Speaker, while reading the bill to incorporate the bank of western Canada and realizing that it comes from the Senate, I cannot but think that the Senate members refused to pass another bill that was requested by all the citizens from a certain province. They bluntly refused, without giving any explanation.
And they expect to bring before the House of Commons an entirely private bill, a bill coming from individuals who request that a bank be added to the eight chartered banks that we already have in Canada.
I do not know whether it is due to the age of the senators, whom I respect, but things have turned topsy-turvy when you begin by refusing what close to two million people ask for and then grant a special favour-because a chartered bank is a special favour-to people like Mr. Coyne and all those whose names are listed here.
Perhaps we will be accused of being against chartered banks. But we are in favour of doing justice to the majority of the people. Now, if the House of Commons were to grant a charter to another bank, I say and I maintain that it should first favour the majority of the population, by complying with a request made by a whole province, before complying with the request of two or three individuals.
We will no doubt be told that several names appear on the list, but we know too well now what a chartered bank is to be fooled by this list of names.
Mr. Speaker, I am not against chartered banks, inasmuch as they remain in their sector. But when they start encroaching on the public sector and especially when this government gives them, by a legal act, the right to accomplish what only a national bank should accomplish, we object.
We are not opposed to the banks themselves, but to the special powers and privileges given to them by former governments. I do not wish to pass judgment on those governments, but they were supposed to administer the business of the country in the interest of the people. Now, I can assure you that

Private Bills
serious questions come to our mind concerning chartered banks.
Mr. Speaker, if we were to increase the present number of chartered banks, what would that change, as long as we maintain that monetary principle, that funny credit? Social Crediters are being accused of wanting to print funny money, but nobody realizes that as it is, we have the funniest monetary credit that ever existed.
Whether we have one, two, three, ten, 20 or 50 agencies issuing credit-I say issuing credit because everybody knows exactly now that the real specialty of chartered banks is to issue new credit-if we always maintain the same monetary system we have today, nothing much will be changed. We might get more competition between those who gamble on the taxpayer because I look at what banks are doing today and I consider them much more as economy gambling houses than as serious accounting institutions whose purpose would be to work in the interests of every citizen.
Besides we cannot blame them for it, because they are private institutions acting for private interests.
But the error of the government is to try to have them play a public part. Precisely, that part should be played by the Bank of Canada. Principles were distorted at that stage by not teaching people what is a real monetary system, because after all a real monetary system, sensibly established, is simply a bookkeeping system.
Today, we of the Social Credit say that this bookkeeping system must be kept by the Bank of Canada and must be nationalized.
If there is one thing that should be national, it is the economic life blood of a nation: its monetary system.
Today they talk about nationalizing everything in the province of Quebec as in other provinces; they nationalize power, they want to nationalize paper mills. It is ridiculous. It is like trying to catch a bear by the tail.
Ministers know it; they cannot speak because undoubtedly their hands are tied, but if they were really sincere and if they worked really for the people and the taxpayer, they would come here to parliament, Mr. Speaker, and they would take steps to free our national economy from all those private financiers who have been fully empowered to empty the taxpayer's pockets.
And if there is one thing that ought to be nationalized by the government, it is surely the monetary system. What do they do today? They say: we have monetary control-be-

cause they read in bulky papers from famous economists that when a country loses 65 per cent of its monetary control, it is bankrupt.
Well, do you know that we, in Canada, only control 10 per cent of our monetary system?
I am wondering if we are not bankrupt three times over because we have lost control of our monetary system at the hands of financiers to whom full powers have been given to control our chartered banks.
We have lost control of over 90 per cent of our credit. In fact, what do we control today? Only the issue of paper money. We control only legal tender, and this control is relatively new, since it dates back to 1934 or thereabouts. Before that-the young people might not remember, but the older people will-each one of the 12 chartered banks in Canada printed its own money. That is why on each bank note appeared the name of the issuing bank-for instance, the provincial bank, the Bank of Montreal, or the names of one of the different banks existing at the time.
On what was the issue of such money based at the time? Each bank had to have in its vaults a gold value equal to the value of the paper money it printed.
You may ask me: What happened that the whole system had to be changed? Well, it happened that they realized that paper money poured from one bank to the other in such quantity that there were monetary surpluses. They realized that there was no more gold in some banks to guarantee the paper money they were issuing.
So the King government, I believe, withdrew from the chartered banks the authorization to print paper money, and ordered that in future only the Bank of Canada would be entitled to issue paper money. And chartered banks were told: if you want paper money, you only have to buy some from the Bank of Canada. And it is still the way it is being done today.
The Bank of Canada has a 100 per cent control over paper money. Should a chartered bank need additional paper money, all it has to do is go to the Bank of Canada and buy the paper money it needs. I am saying this because as far as legal tender is concerned, the chartered bank is playing what is really its part.
The chartered bank is an institution dealing with money; it does not create money. Chartered banks are essential to the over-all economy of this country, but only as far as they play their part, which consists in money dealings. When they use their customers'

Private Bills
deposits to make loans, everything is right. If they do not have enough, they buy some from the central bank in order to lend it at low interest rates. Such is the part chartered banks must play.
As long as chartered banks will not resume playing their proper part, Canada will get more and more into debt, because as long as Canada will only control part of its money supply, which is the legal currency, and will allow the monetary credit, that is, the balance of the money supply, to be controlled, as long as chartered banks will be allowed to issue or create this new monetary credit out of nothing, as long as this government will allow private enterprise to create the assets of the country and to lend it again to the country, I say that a tremendous theft is being committed and parliament is responsible for it before the country. In my opinion, this is a wrong that must be righted.
If in order to correct the legal monetary system the government of that time had to resort to drastic measures to gain a 100 per cent control over its legal currency, if it had to temporarily prohibit all banks and impose new conditions on them, I say that the remedy which was good at that time for the legal currency is good today for monetary credit.
Before 1934 we had lost control of legal currency; today we have lost control of monetary credit. Control of our credit must be regained. Such is the remedy; the means used to regain control of legal currency should be used again.
Then any new credit created in Canada will really be for Canada. For instance, if next year Canada has a capital gain, a net revenue, a surplus, or is richer by more than $10 billion, the amount should be credited to the Bank of Canada, which is the people's bank, the bank of each and every citizen. If instead of giving those $10 billion back to chartered banks so that they may circulate it, they were credited to the Bank of Canada to be used for the welfare of Canadian citizens, I can tell you that in four or five years from now, we would no longer hear about the debt system that we have today.
Suppose that next year we have a capital gain of $10 billion. With that amount, I think we could start by "paying our way", cover our budget expenditures and still have a balance of $3 billion.
But what is being done today to help the average citizen who had the heart to work day and night for the further development
of the country, even with the help of machines and science?
What do we do in point of fact? We say to international financial organizations: Get hold of this production, get hold of the country's net assets and lend it back to the citizens, school boards, municipalities, provinces and even the federal government, while the next day we are being taxed to fully cover budget expenditures, deductions being made from our cheques, while all the revenues of the country are going directly into the hands of international financiers.
Such is our economic situation; such are the results of those special privileges granted to the chartered banks. Those banks are private establishments which have been given the extensive powers of public enterprise. They have been given all the powers the government has for extending new credit. And today there is but one solution: to get into debt.
As my friend was saying a while ago, there was once a fellow who had won $3,000. Overjoyed, he ran to this neighbour and told him: "Here, take this money. I can't look after it, it's too complicated. Tomorrow, I'll come and borrow it from you, with interest." That is exactly what is happening with the chartered banks. We can get out of this impasse if we stop saying we have to get into debt.
If we have to get into debt, it is because we live under a crazy system. That is the only reason why people get into debt. Do not think for a second that Canada is not rich enough to feed a mere 19 million inhabitants.
I am convinced that if our economy were truly strong, our fellow citizens could get what is rightly theirs. For that to happen, however, Canada would need to have its own bookkeeping system.
In short, the only way to achieve that end would be for the Bank of Canada to have full control over such bookkeeping.
As long as chartered banks are not forced to operate on a 100 per cent liquid basis, all other reforms will be useless. That is what we want and that is what the government must require-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I regret to interrupt the hon. member but his time has expired.

Mr. Speaker, I do not think there could be a better example of putting the cart before the horse than the introduction of this bill into the house at this time. The house is charged

Private Bills
with the responsibility of taking action on the report of the royal commission on banking, as well as revising the Bank Act next year. Yet at the same time we find the government bringing forward measures which would allow the establishment of, not one, not two but possibly three new banking institutions in this country. Before any action is taken by the house with regard to the establishment of new banking institutions, surely we should have some appreciation of what the government intends to do about the report of the royal commission on banking, and what it intends to do in respect of the revision of the Bank Act next year.
I do not believe it is fair at this time to ask members to approve or disapprove of the establishment of one, two or three new banking institutions when we are not fully cognizant of what the government intends to do with regard to the Bank Act. At the same time, it is my personal opinion that we have no great need for the establishment of new banking institutions in this country. Indeed in recent years we have witnessed the merging of various substantial banking institutions with other banking institutions. I am not referring to banking institutions that have been in existence for one or two years, but those that have been in existence for a great number of years and have a broadly based business in this country. Yet these institutions felt it was necessary to amalgamate with other institutions in order to get a still broader base so that they could compete in a satisfactory manner for the banking business of this country. With this point of view in mind, I feel we should take a very long look at these bills before we allow further institutions of this nature to be established in this country.
Now, it seems to me that the government did not want to face this issue, that it did not want to make any specific decision as to whether or not there was a need for more banking institutions. The government has allowed a large number of people to spend a great deal of money in endeavouring to establish new institutions of this nature in Canada. The government is now in the unfortunate and unfavourable position of having to make a decision which they would rather not make. It would appear to me that we will meet with no success during this session in attempting to pass any of these bills. For this reason, and for the very obvious reason that the Bank Act has to be revised, I feel it would be much wiser if these bills were withdrawn until such time as we, as members of this

house, know exactly what the government's intentions are with regard to the Bank Act.
There is a further problem here and it is a very important one; it is one that will weigh heavily upon the mind of each member as he considers this matter. As I pointed out, we have seen banking institutions amalgamating in this country on numerous occasions in the past few years. It would be a most unfortunate thing if we were to approve the establishment of these banks, then find out within a year or two that their boards of directors decided they should amalgamate with some other bank that is presently in existence and has available a broad base of branches across this nation which are providing a service the people need and like. As a result of this we would find a few people reaping huge benefits in the way of profits because we, as members of parliament, had approved the establishment of these institutions before we were fully cognizant of all the facts related to them.
This is the type of decision that I am sure members would just as soon not be saddled with. Certainly I am in that position. I have not learned that there is any lack of availability of credit through the existing banking institutions. As a matter of fact it has always been my opinion that we probably have the best banking system in the world. We have a system which provides service through branches to communities which, under any other type of system, could not look forward to having a branch bank in their community. This has resulted, in the main, from the fact that we have had a small number of banks with a large number of branches which have been in a position to build up this type of support right across the nation, and the type of financial backing that allowed them to suffer losses in some areas because of the benefits they were able to derive from other areas.
We have a sound system. I would not like to think we would do anything to damage this banking system in any way. At the same time if it is proven to me that we have no fear from the establishment of a new banking institution in this country, that it will provide benefits that are not available now to the Canadian people, that the competition would be of benefit to everyone concerned, then certainly I would be quite willing to give my approval to the establishment of a new bank. However, I feel there are a lot of questions to be answered and that we should not be establishing new banking institutions on an ad hoc basis. I feel this question should be part of the government's revision of the

Bank Act, in association with the royal commission report on banking. Until this is presented to us by the government of the day I do not believe we, as a parliament, should be charged with making a decision on the bill before us, or on the other two bills which I believe are ready to come before us.
Before another private members' hour comes up, Mr. Speaker, I hope the government will give some thought to this problem so that we will not spend another hour on this bill. We should know the long range plans of the government in relation to the Bank Act in general before this bill is considered further.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order; the hour appointed for private members' business has expired.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at 8 p.m.

The house resumed consideration of the motion by Mr. Pearson:
That the government be authorized to take such steps as may be necessary to establish officially as the flag of Canada a flag embodying the emblem proclaimed by His Majesty King George V on November 21, 1921-three maple leaves conjoined on one stem-in the colours red and white then designated for Canada, the red leaves occupying a field of white between vertical sections of blue on the edges of the flag.
And the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Diefenbaker, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Churchill.

Mr. Speaker, I had a few minutes start before private members' hour, but I think it would do no harm to remind the house that the gist of my remarks is simply that the government is going about this flag resolution in the wrong way, that there now seems to be stiffening of attitude, that there does not seem to be any desire to meet half way, and this in face of the fact that there is no explanation why the government should give the matter such haste and urgency, and that no one has been able to explain to the house or to the people of Canada why a flag design must be rammed through.
I do not want to be just negative. It is my contention, Mr. Speaker, that this resolution, or these resolutions, really, should be turned
Canadian Flag
over to a committee of the house. I do not agree with the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson) that 15 members would do;
I think it should be a good sized committee. Most of our committees consist of 60 members. Many of them have difficulty getting a quorum, and I can only imagine the difficulty of the task imposed on just 15 trying to be there all the time, especially when some seem to be so desirous of speed, as we have seen evidence to that effect.
It is my purpose this evening to point out to the house, in perhaps a more emphatic manner than I did before, the results already observable in the country because of the Prime Minister's determination to force a choice of a flag down the throats of the people of Canada. I say the situation is getting worse because the government persists, even though there is plenty of evidence to show that aside from having a majority of the people of Canada in favour of the flag there is much evidence to indicate that a majority are against it.
The hon. member for Red Deer mentioned the low repute into which parliament is falling. I can only repeat the words of the hon. member for Mackenzie (MT. Korchinski), who said it so well, that this is the government's doing. It is the government which has the responsibility of bringing on business. It is the government that wanted to introduce this flag. It is the government which has so many pieces of legislation on the order paper, and it is entirely in the government's hands whether it wants to proceed with those measures which will cure some of the ills of the country or proceed with this one measure which it thinks will be such a political gimmick and palliative to many who are in economic difficulty. The effect on the country is simply that, and I suspect partly it is because the government is so slow in doing anything for the province of Quebec.
The previous government was berated by some of our members from eastern Canada, Ontario and Quebec, because they had felt that the western farmer had been given too much attention, that too much had been done for him and not enough for the other farmers. There is much evidence to show that the small Quebec farmer is in almost desperate straits. He needs the type of action which the former government gave. He is looking to the present government for that type of action. I would think part of the difficulty here is that everybody across Canada, especially in the west of Canada, knows so well that what this government is doing is substituting politics for government-

Canadian Flag
Hear, hear.

-asking the people to accept a banner instead of the concrete action that they have waited for so long.
As I think I mentioned previously, a parallel situation would have been the awful plight the western fanners would have met in the last three years by asking them to put a sheaf of wheat on the red ensign, and wave that to show how much the government thought of the farmers. That is what this government is doing to the Quebec farmer.
I suggest that trying to convince the people of Quebec that, because we are holding up this flag debate we are stopping all necessary legislation, is a lie so big it can only be credited to that party which has the greatest success in selling lies to the country, the Liberal party. I want to assure the house that I have had no part in trying to lend any fuel to divisive thought in the country. In my last speech I only mentioned part of a couple of letters, but I do feel my duty to the house is to represent as fully and completely as I can the type of feelings which, as I say, are the result of the way in which the government is now proceeding, and to ask the government again to reconsider.
I had mentioned the first paragraph of an article on page 4 of the Edmonton Journal. Now I am going to read a considerable part of it because I am sure many members of the house will be shocked at its tone, will be surprised at its vehemence. I know through private conversation with some of my Canadian friends of French origin that they found it almost incredible, but they finally had to accept that such is the result of the way in which the government is trying to foist this flag on Canada.
I feel the house should be subjected to the reading of this, in order to give it a little second thought on how we are proceeding. With the permission of the house I shall reread the first paragraph:
I suggest that the "blackmailed" Liberal government of Mr. L. B. Pearson has done more to dissolve confederation than any group could have done had it deliberately set out to accomplish this fact.
In their bid to buy the 75 Quebec seats, the Liberals dropped Canadian politics to a new low by appealing to the nationalistic spirit of the French.
Irresponsible and unconstitutional promises bought them a Quebec majority at the expense of Canada. Cowering to pressure from Quebec has won the Liberals the support of French speaking M.P.'s regardless of political affiliation.
Liberal strategists who formulate policy might well have provided their minions with calling cards with the legend "Have tails, will grovel."

I think the hon. member for Jasper-Edson (Mr. Horner) mentioned that paragraph the other night. While I believe I should put this on the record because I think it is so scandalous, I hasten to assure the house that these are not my feelings, but the only way in which I am sure the Edmonton Journal could be persuaded to print this kind of article at all is because that newspaper is aware that this sort of feeling is being expressed more and more in the country.
I would remind the house of the Prime Minister's words when he said that what a flag should do is unify the country, and that it should be a unifying banner. I wish the Prime Minister had explained to the house how his unifying banner is going to patch up all this. To continue this article:
The Liberal government has opened a Canadian Pandora's box which it cannot close. We have the spectacle of a federal government that is controlled by Quebec.
Certainly, that reflects a feeling in this country as a result of the actions of a government which, without explanation and contrary to all common sense, contrary to the feeling of parliament and in place of other methods such as trying to get co-operation from other parties, has attempted to ram this decision through. This is bound to give rise to some suspicion, when one considers the predominant number of Quebec ministers in the cabinet, that the Prime Minister has his hands tied-that this resolution must go through, no matter what happens.
French Canadians to a great extent feel strongly that we should have a new flag. This feeling is common knowledge. In the absence of any explanation from the government these circumstances are bound to lead to a feeling that the Prime Minister has had his nose twisted by the Quebec ministers. I suggest that whether this be true or false, and no matter how anxious these people are to have their flag design go through, no responsible prime minister could see such a feeling grow, or observe the divisive effects of this feeling across the country and not realize that its actions are doing more to divide Canada than any flag could unify it.
I am paying particular attention to this article in the Edmonton Journal because it appeared in a paper which has usually supported the Liberals at election time and which has not been too kind to Conservatives in connection with the flag debate. I suggest, again, that it must have some meaning or

this newspaper would not have given it such prominence. It continues:
We have a federal government that intends to force the rest of Canada to accept changes in the B.N.A. Act that will make Canada a bilingual country and accordingly perpetuate the life of the Liberal government.
There are those who would have us believe that Canada is a bilingual nation.
We are not, nor was it the intention of the authors of the B.N.A. Act to make French a second language for Canadians.
The use of French in Canada has caused us all concern from time to time. We have seen its use greatly expanding. No parliament can compare with this one for the manner in which French speaking Canadians have insisted at every opportunity that French be given an equal place in this house. I would say, too, that there has been no resistance to this trend, except on occasions such as when a committee has been unable to provide a simultaneous translation system, when we felt that the French Canadians could all understand English, though the reverse was not true, and that in the interest of co-operation they might have shown a little less insistence. I can understand the feeling of our French Canadian members that any slackening of their demands would be taken as an indication of bad faith by their constituents. However, I feel they have a responsibility in this house now and then to lead public opinion and not be driven by it to unreasonable lengths. I suggest that more friends are won by reasonableness and compromise, by pointing out an unfairness, than by taking up the club and saying: We will have this, or else.
I know that despite what is said in this article and despite the expressions of opinion in some of the letters I get from my constituents, the ordinary Canadian in Alberta, in my area, would feel nothing but a sense of outrage if he felt that French speaking Canadians were being discriminated against. I would remind the house of something which took place not too long ago. When the railway committee made a fuss about the manner in which promotions were handled by the Canadian National Railways, the president of the railway said he would have an investigation conducted and the situation would be corrected. And he did. He brought in some new rules, and in the following year there was no trouble with the committee whatsoever. The lesson, therefore, is that there are certain areas in which there may be legitimate grievances, and when these grievances are brought forward reasonable men will listen to them .and give effect to changes which will correct
Canadian Flag
the position and do away with any feeling that people are not being treated fairly. People in western Canada can understand the desire of French Canadians for justice where they think it is being denied. This is in accordance with a theme I have often pursued in this house-the people must be heard; their voice must be listened to. It is in this light that I ask the house to consider the feelings of those who live in my area respecting the manner in which this flag question is being handled and the attempt which is made to ram it through without sufficient consideration for their point of view.
I have referred before in this house to the tendency in western Canada in depression days to blame the "Bay street boys". The flag is only a symbol of our country, after all. It is the health of the nation, the position of each citizen, no matter what his ethnic origin, that really matters. It is the duty of the government to pay heed to the economic wellbeing of the nation rather than to political propaganda associated with this issue.
Now I should like to continue reading a little further from this article. The heading is "Bilingual?"
Section 133 of the B.N.A. Act clearly states that French is an official language in Canada only for the purpose of debates in parliament, the provincial legislature of Quebec, the official records of these governments, proceedings in the Supreme Court of Canada, Quebec provincial courts and the Exchequer Court of Canada.
I say that the French language has no official or legal status in any other area of Canada.
May I say that my constituency contains only a small percentage of French speaking Canadians. Despite the fact that I get very few votes from these particular electors, I have some close friends among them. I have been here in parliament for six and a half years and I have never heard any voice raised by these people telling me they were afraid they would lose their language or their religion. I never heard any expression of opinion from any of them that they were being treated as inferior Canadians. I know they use the French language in their homes, and that their children speak it. I know they are brought up to be Catholics and I know they get along very well with their English speaking neighbours across the road. My fear is that it will be very much more difficult for them to do so, should the government persist in the kind of action it is now taking.
Why does the government try to divide Canada at this time? What is wrong with doing the normal business of parliament in

Canadian Flag
this house? Why cannot we treat the flag resolution as any other resolution and debate it in this house in the same manner, with all members having the guts to stand up and speak their piece?
Hear, hear.

Then send it to a committee, which can do its work in a worth-while and efficient manner and report back to the house in due course? Where are all those of so little faith in this house? I suggest that if the parliament of Canada is falling into disrepute with the people of this country, it is because of the calculated campaign in that regard by the Liberal government, which always feels that the way to perpetuate a Liberal government in power is to downgrade parliament so that legitimate criticism will receive little attention from the nation.
Where are those voices in the Liberal back benches that go home and make such a great pretence to their constituents that they are looking after their affairs? They have not the nerve to stand up in this house and refute those arguments which we say are legitimate criticisms of the manner in which this issue is being handled by the government. Why cannot members who feel strongly about the flag get up and tell us why? Why is there no voice from the province of Quebec that will interpret the feeling in that province to the rest of Canada, so there might be understanding? Where are these pseudo spokesmen from Quebec? Why are they afraid to get up and explain their stand?
The hon. member for St. Denis (Mr. Pru-d'homme) had the effrontery the last time I was speaking to ask whether I have explained to my constituents what Quebeckers want. I pointed out to him that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) and other Quebec members in this house have not yet told us or explained what the people in that province want. Is it not time, Mr. Speaker, for those who want a symbol that is not wanted by most of Canada to explain to us the meaning of that symbol; to explain to us exactly what new type of Canadianism they think a new type of flag will signify? My constituents are reasonable people. If you have a reasonable argument, they have the right to hear it; and I want them to hear it. You show us some reason, and they will buy it. I say to the government they are not going to shove this flag down the throats of the people of Canada when the majority of the people do not want it.
Hear, hear.

We are not going to abandon our duty to fight that kind of tactic and that particular flag. I would suggest that instead of just standing here talking, from now on there should be no estimates passed, no supply passed, no money granted this government until it decides that the voice of the people of this country shall be heard.
Hear, hear.

I am challenging my friends
opposite to bring forward the reason; to get up in this house and debate this issue. I ask them to point out the fault in my reasoning, to explain to us and to the people of Canada the Prime Minister's method of handling this matter. Let those members from the province of Quebec who are most vehement and most concerned about it explain to the rest of Canada the injustice that must be corrected and how this new symbol will do it. The people of Canada are entitled to at least that much. I say again, Mr. Speaker, that I for one am getting just a little fed up with just delaying this matter. If the government does not want to get on with essential business, I for one want to grant that government no more money. It is not fit to carry on as a government of this country.
Oh, oh.

You may all think I am on the wrong side in this matter and that if this were to result in an election I might be defeated. But I will tell you something. I will have been defeated as an honest man; and I wonder how many of those silent members over there could go home with the same feeling of honesty and patriotism.
I am not going to read the rest of this article, Mr. Speaker, but I want to remind the house that it is something I have read. This appears in the only daily newspaper in the northern part of Alberta. I say it was printed because a great deal more of that feeling has appeared-and that feeling has only come about in the last little while. I ask the government backbenchers over there, is that what you want to do to Canada? I am reporting to my constituents that this is a deliberate plot on the part of the Liberals to do just that to Canada. I hope there is an election soon and that I will get a Liberal opponent like one of those hon. gentlemen opposite to run against me, because on every public platform I would love to tell this story to my constituents.

Mr. Speaker, like previous speakers in this rather prolonged

debate, I plan to place before the house a proposal with regard to which I hope all members will take an opportunity to express themselves. Before I do so I would like to express some views, a few of them personal and some of them partisan in the sense that I speak for my colleagues in the debate. The personal remarks really deal with my regrets over some of the overtones that have been brought in by some of my Conservative colleagues relating, for example, to French Canada.
Oh, oh.
You are one to talk.
The hon. member from Alberta says, "You are one to talk". He is quite aware that I am not the most popular political figure in the province of Quebec.
Or anywhere else.
Trying to make it up, eh?

But the point is that I happen to be one of those who were prepared to vote for the new flag, and I am not one of those who consider it is any concession to Quebec or French Canada. I am sure I have the right as much as anyone else to say that. The second point I wanted to make is also a reaction to what I think has been an unnecessary wrapping of patriotism and chauvinism around the support of the red ensign. I have nothing against the flag, but I have heard so much about the red ensign waving in shot and shell and our soldiers dying and fighting for it. Maybe symbolically there is something in this; but I had a fair measure of experience in one war and I was certainly around the front a great deal, and I only remember seeing the red ensign in view in two places-one was on General Simonds' Staghound that he used to trundle his way around in, and the other was on a Canadian corps headquarters tent. I never saw it any other place.
I wanted to make this point because there seems to be an attempt to generate the opinion that our soldiers were in action with the red ensign fluttering, in a sense, as their national symbol. It seems that people who try to accentuate that point of view make a mistake about what was the character of recent wars. I would also like them to consider what the character of future wars may be, if they are thinking of a flag solely in terms of a military symbol around which to rally.
The other personal point I wanted to make has to do with the tendency of our Conserv-

ative colleagues who have dominated the debate in the sense of the number of contributions. This is very much a personal reaction and has nothing to do with the issue before us. I could have forgiven them a lot easier if in their speeches they had been less ready to pat themselves on the back for the quality of those speeches. It is a minor point but I wanted to put it to you.
Mr. Speaker, I should like now to turn to the more general points. We are now going to have a free vote.
Oh, yes.

I should like to point out to my hon. friends that the Prime Minister made that clear in the form of a statement, which I think was a concession in this house, which we certainly took in our group as meaning there would be a free vote which would depend on our individual consciences. I think everyone here is aware that the sum of the consciences of our particular parliamentary group does not add up to the total of promised support. There are a number of our members who are prepared to support the red ensign while a number are prepared to support the new flag.
Would the hon. member permit a question?

No, I will not permit a question, Mr. Speaker. This willingness to compromise is not something in which we have any special righteousness. I do not believe, however, that the proposals which were put forward by the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Scott), in connection with the design, and by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), in connection with parliamentary procedure, or by my leader in connection with arrangements for a house leaders' meeting, have been mere ploys in a partisan game, or represent anything underhanded or opportunistic from our own point of view in this particular issue.
Throughout the development of this issue from the fateful evening reception of the press-specially selected-by the Prime Minister, through his Winnipeg appearance, which I much regret, before the Legion; through the introduction of the resolutions; the early debate; its temporary hoisting; through the long summer; through the long and continuing interim supply debate, which prefaced this present debate, until we got into the four days a week continuity of debate, and throughout this whole business, until we are now debating very broadly a rather narrow

Canadian Flag
subamendment moved by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill)- through all this we have been somewhat unwilling watchers of the confrontation between the government's determination to have a flag and the official opposition's determination to block it. I think a substantial majority of the official opposition is obdurate and wants or intends to block it.
We have heard the stories about 14 more amendments to follow. I do not know whether there is any substance in them or not, but I assume that my hon. friends in the opposition are determined, as evidenced by the remarks of the last speaker. Just today during the question period we were told that there was no change in the government's position. Just today the Prime Minister told us he knew nothing about any private negotiations between the major parties' representatives for a way out of this dilemma.
I am chary of saying I speak for the Canadian people or any portion of them in this debate, after hearing from my hon. friends, with a repetition which makes me despair, that they speak for thousands, and even millions. I am hesitant to talk about history, even though I have been a history teacher, after listening to some of the historical interpretations of my hon. friends, some of which have given me a different and unusual light on events back to and including the Norman conquest.
I am not anxious to dwell on the issues of parliamentary efficiency or filibuster, or whether this is just a noble sense of duty that is being displayed. I do not feel that I should go into that in any great detail; but I believe that one substantial body of opinion in this country has not been well represented by spokesmen in this debate. This opinion, at its most radical, is that we in parliament in this debate are making fools of the electors. This opinion, at its mildest, is querulous and confused over what is going on. Or, putting it simply, it demands: When are you going to get down to business; when are you going to tackle laws and spending items which mean something to me?
Get down to business; get on with it. Let me put a plea to the government and the official opposition. Your confrontation is not helping parliament. Your stubbornness is not helping the cause of the federal government at this particular time when we have burgeoning provincialism. This may not be so dramatic as saying, a plague on both your houses; but I certainly feel in respect of this

particular issue, each side of this confrontation has egg on its face.
While we sit and listen and listen, and some talk, ostensibly to this subamendment on the voting procedure of a plebiscite, a lot of things are not being considered which we believe should be considered. Look at the order paper. Even the measure we most want, the Canada pension legislation outline, is not on it. There is only an expression of the intention of the government.
Mr. Speaker, I wonder whether the hon. gentleman will permit a question?
No, Mr. Speaker, I will not permit a question.

Oh, oh.
He is one of the kissing cousins and has finally come around.

Order. The hon. member has asked a very pertinent question on the point of order, but I point out to him that all hon. members have been allowed a great deal of leeway in their opening remarks. It does seem to me that during this type of debate an hon. member is entitled to honestly give his own opinions in this house, which is a forum and not a courtroom.

Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to press the point of order at all. I understand Your Honour has made a ruling, but I wonder whether the hon. gentleman can tell us when this fine act of co-operation was developed, because I have noticed the Liberal members opposite seem ready for what the hon. member is about to announce.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say that the hon. gentleman is in for one big surprise.
We know what is coming.
We know what is going on.

Mr. Speaker, I should just like to say to you that we have a subamendment before us which in effect would put the suggested plebiscite on a national scale in such a way that there would be no local counting of votes. I think we should be considering the Department of Forestry rather than this item.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that people who want to search for principles under which to stand should look at redistribution legislation, which in itself is a principle that we are denying by our inattention. When the prospect is before us that we will possibly be fighting an election on the basis of 1951, what greater sacrilege could be committed? What greater sacrilegious move could one make in the parliamentary process than by putting off or postponing legislation of the type I mentioned?
With all the talk we have heard, the time of parliament is fleeting and this session is moving toward an end. I suppose this parliament is moving toward an end. We are at an impasse. We are in a state of legislative paralysis. I do not want to overwork this word "sincerity", which people have been throwing around, but with some sincerity we have debated this whole question in respect of that which this country wishes us to do. We believe the country wants us to get about our business. If the opposition will not let us move the flag issue along to a vote; if it will not accept a compromise in the form of a committee and then a limited debate; if the government insists, as it does, that it cannot go any further in the way of concessions, then there is nothing much we can do to register our opinion that we should be looking after the business of this country that is before us on the order paper, or has been promised for the order paper, than to make the move I now make.
If we did this, at the very least it would put the spotlight on who among us want to tackle more substantial and I think less deflated matters.
