Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate on the 
subamendment I think my first remarks should be directed through you to the hon. members across the way who tonight have shown that they have discernment and good taste, and that they really appreciate the remarks that have been made by members of the official opposition and others on this side of the house who have taken part in this debate so far. One of the remarkable things about what has happened tonight relates to the entrance of the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) to take part in the vote, accompanied by many members of the cabinet who, as soon as the vote had taken place-a vote in which they indicated they wanted a continuation of this debate-immediately left the house.
Hear hear.

Mr. Speaker, I am rising on a question of privilege. I am sure the hon. member for Rosthern would not have wanted to make that remark had he realized that the Prime Minister was presiding as host at a dinner for the delegates to the commonwealth educational conference and that the ministers who came back for the division interrupted their dinner to come here to vote.
Oh, oh.
Well, Mr. Speaker, if hon. gentlemen feel that is the kind of exhibition they want to put on for our guests from other countries, I cannot share that view.
Oh, oh.

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the Minister of Transport for the remarks he has made. Of course I agree that the Prime Minister has a responsibility to be where he is tonight, if the minister's remarks are according to the facts.
Oh, oh.
Shame.
Mr. Speaker, I certainly do not want to cast any reflection on the Minister of Transport-
Oh, no?

-and I sincerely want to make that perfectly plain. If what he has said is so, I wonder why the members of the Prime Minister's party voted the way they did tonight. To me it indicates they have no legislation to bring before the House of Commons.
Order. I do hope the hon. member will not continue along that line, because his last few remarks were really out of order.
They are true but they are out of order.
We have had a vote tonight that will be remembered in the history of this parliament.
Order.

Those who cry filibuster, those who cry obstruction, what was their cry tonight? They wanted more of the same. Speaking in the debate tonight the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) referred to those pieces of legislation for which the country is crying. What was the answer from members across the way? They want a continuation of a debate they have called futile, a debate they have called damaging to the image of parliament and to the welfare of the country. I do not want to say anything more along that line, except to note that they had some notable allies in the vote that took place tonight.
Where were your Quebec members?

This debate has been one of the most dynamic in the six years that I have been a member of the House of Commons. I was never prouder to be a member of this party and to be associated with those on this side of the house than I was yesterday when the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) placed upon the record some of the history of this country. He spoke as one who appreciates those things that are built into the traditions of a people, those things that went into the building not only of the part of the country with which he has been associated but also every part of this nation, as he put forward the case for the flag that throughout the world today is known as the Canadian flag.
Every morning when I have come to the parliament buildings while the commonwealth educational conference has been in session and have passed the front of the west block I have seen the flags of the commonwealth there, and I know in my heart as every Canadian knows that the Canadian red ensign is a distinctive flag not to be-
Not to be.

-not to be mistaken for any other flag. Mr. Speaker, there are some across the way whom I would like to see
20220-483i
Canadian Flag
on their feet giving the reasons why they believe Canadians should accept the three maple leaf flag. After all, we have not heard any arguments from the other side of the house indicating why the three maple leaf flag should be the flag of this country.
The other day the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) placed upon the record some proposals that he thought might be a solution to the impasse that now faces parliament, and to an even greater extent the Canadian people. I believe he spoke as one who had made a reasonable and forthright appraisal of the situation that exists in this nation today. I think he also showed he had an appreciation of the history involved in the building of this nation from the very earliest times. All of these things have contributed and are contributing to a developing situation in Canada from which I believe those who support the Prime Minister and his personal flag can take very little comfort.
I remember the words of the Prime Minister when he put the resolution before the House of Commons. If I understood his remarks correctly, he thought that this measure was necessary if we were to have an increased degree of unity in the country. I also recall the early days of the debate on the measure and remember those who said that perhaps it was already too late to bring forward such a measure. We have seen the transformation that has taken place across the nation. Many were prepared to support the new flag, many thought that perhaps there was some good in this measure, but every day we see the opposition to it increasing from one end of the nation to the other. That is one of the reasons we have the subamendment before the house at the present time.
Hon. members will recall that prior to the last general election campaign there were those who said they had the answers to the problems that confronted the nation. There were those who said that the prime minister of that day, now Leader of the Opposition, was unable to meet the challenge of the problems that faced the nation. An election was held and a minority government was elected. I want to place on the record at this point what they said when they were elected, as found in the Ottawa Citizen for April 18, 1963:
Lester Pearson and his ministers will come to power equipped with sheaves of policy papers, priority lists and agendas which they expect will enable the quickest take-off of any new government in Canadian history. One Liberal backroom boy, flipping through a neatly bound and confidential Pearson program guide, commented, "No party ever came into office as well prepared to draft

Canadian Flag
legislation and take executive action". The business of fining down broad party policy into programs which should be put into effect has been going on for years.
This was the situation when this government came into office. You will recall the legislation that was brought forward after 60 days of decision. You will recall the time that was wasted. Again tonight we have had an example of a government that is not prepared to meet parliament with legislation. I maintain, sir, that this is no longer a matter of simple determination when you take into consideration the question that this parliament is being asked to consider at the moment. It is no longer a matter of those things of which the Prime Minister spoke when he introduced this legislation. It is a matter of trying to salvage something out of national unity. This is the challenge that faces the Prime Minister and the government. I say this to the Prime Minister and to those around him: He never faced a greater challenge. He will never face a greater challenge in his career. The people of this country are watching and waiting to see if he is equal to that challenge. None of us is so faultless that he has never made a mistake. None of us is so faultless that he has not something in the past of which he is not altogether proud. On this occasion, although there may be an element of that kind facing the Prime Minister, surely in the name of national unity, for the welfare of this nation and the generations that will follow, this Prime Minister has the courage, the decisiveness necessary to make a decision that will bring this parliament back to active consideration of a legislative program that will give the people of this country the instruments of unity through the economic use of the resources this nation has.
There are those who say that a plebiscite is not the answer. I remember the plebiscite of those other days. I remember the way it was brought about. I remember too what followed that plebiscite. I remember the animosities and those other intangible questions that were left in the mind of one Canadian as he faced another Canadian. This is one of the reasons we have the subamendment before this house moved by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill). We are trying to prevent that kind of thing from happening in Canada again. There is no one on the other side of the house who, in his heart, does not know that this is the course which should be followed in connection with a matter as important as the one before us now.
There are other aspects of this problem with which I should like to deal as well. In thinking of the whole problem of national unity, thinking of the problem of trying to decide what shall be the flag of this nation, I find myself confused by the action that has been taken by the government in proposing a two pronged resolution which promises the people of this nation two flags. Every one of us in this house knows that the union jack is the flag of Great Britain. There is no need to pass a resolution in this parliament to recognize Great Britain as the head of the commonwealth. I am a little shocked, and I am a little sad too, to think that he who is the Prime Minister of this country would try to introduce a measure of such shallow consequences before this parliament and before the Canadian people in an effort to try to justify one section of the proposal he has made.
The other day the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton (Mr. Flemming) brought up the matter of the amenities that should exist as between one province and another in deciding on a distinctive Canadian flag. I think he brought forcibly to our attention the fact that confederation means more than the simple terms embodied in that act. After all, there will always be an argumentative situation in this connection, but there are some things that belong to the provinces, while other fields belong to the federal government. In a matter of such importance as the flag, surely there should have been consultations with the provinces to secure their views before any design was placed before parliament.
I see the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Des-chatelets) smiling. I do not believe that a minister representing the province of Quebec-
No, no, on a point of order-
-should be smiling at this reference.
I rise on a point of order, Mr. Speaker. I was not smiling; I was laughing.

Then, the greater is the shame that a minister representing a province containing a third of the population of this country, a province that has fought for provincial rights down through the years, a province that has held out for those things distinctive in its own life, should smile at a reference such as I made in regard to the


amenities that should exist as between the provinces and the federal government.
Of course, when I think of the resolution now before us, the amendment and the subamendment, I think of my own riding which is one of the historic ridings of this country. It is a riding composed of people of many origins. I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Korchinski) upon the speech he made this afternoon. I must confess that it would be a poor Canadian, it would be a poor member of parliament indeed, who did not approach this subject with some measure of hesitation. After all, we all know that in a matter such as this there is a variety of opinion. There is a widespread division in this country. There is a widespread division between some of the ethnic groups. As I look at my one constituency, as I think of the correspondence I have received and as I recall the visit I made to my riding, I am moved to reinforce some of those things that have been said in this debate.
Five years ago, four years ago, three years ago, perhaps even two years ago, you did not find in western Canada what you find there today. You did not find any animosity toward the province of Quebec. I want to remind hon. members that during the period when the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) was prime minister some actions were taken that were not altogether of a non-controversial nature. I remember one of those-the adoption of bilingual cheques. There was not a murmur from any place in Canada when that action was taken, but what would have been the situation had there been the manoeuvring at that particular time of a government like the one we have opposite? They would have fed the fires of isolation, as they have always fed the fires of isolation.
Hear, hear.
Explain.

Somebody says "explain". I could talk here all night and explain, and you would not know any more than you know now. Some people have a closed mind when it comes to taking a look at the aspirations of Canadians in all parts of the nation.
I recall that when I first came to the House of Commons I was very conscious of the fact that the people from whom I descended had not been in Canada very long. My father came to Canada from Lebanon. My mother was born in Canada of Swedish parents, and I remember the community in which we lived and in which we were a minority-I would
Canadian Flag
say a very minor minority. I can recall first going to school, and I think many other hon. members who were in the same situation can remember some of those experiences too. I believe I know something about what minorities in this country have faced over the years.
Later on, as the years rolled by, I became interested in politics. One could not help but become interested in politics in western Canada when we had a government here in Ottawa that for so many years neglected the problems of western Canada.
Hear, hear.
You know, Mr. Speaker, they were so negligent that a socialist government was elected in our province for the first time and in the first place anywhere on the North American continent.
In what year?

1944. As I recall, the first campaign in which I took part, in 1953, was the first time I had a chance to become acquainted with some of the French speaking people in my riding, and I have 1,500 of them. I want to say they are among the best farmers and businessmen to be found in that riding.
Hear, hear.

When I go back to my riding, as I did a week ago, and find people of other origins pointing their fingers at them because of the actions taken by this government, I know someone has not been working for national unity.
Hear, hear.
That situation did not exist five, four, three, even two years ago.
Six months ago.

Well, I think that we could go a little further back than that because, after all, there have been other actions that have been the most divisive in the entire history of this country.
I recall the remarks made in this debate by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp), and it was he who referred to a troublesome minority. It was he who referred to appeasement-and these are not words for a minister of the crown. But what do concern me at the moment are the actions of some of those on the treasury benches opposite. I wish they were here tonight so that they might hear what I have to say, although I know that they know all about

Canadian Flag
these things, having been responsible for the clippings I want to refer to very briefly.
I do so, sir, not to try to stray away from this subject but to try to keep to the theme of national unity, the influence that a flag can have, the necessity today of taking the action proposed by this party of having a plebiscite because the actions taken by the Prime Minister have ruled out any other possibility, unless he still has in the back of his mind the sending of this measure to a committee of the house for consideration.
Here in Canada we expect leadership from those who are given responsibility. There are no officers of the house who are given more responsibility than those who sit behind the Prime Minister on the cabinet benches. Now I want to refer to a quotation from the Winnipeg Tribune of April 4. This is what one cabinet minister has been going around the country saying:
If Quebec leaves confederation western Canada will be forced to its knees, begging for help and aid from Washington-
This is a quotation from a cabinet minister, the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Teillet).
Shame.

Then he went on to say this:
He warned his audience if the present situation between Quebec and the rest of Canada is allowed to continue, confederation will be dissolved.
Where did this talk of separation start? It started right in the cabinet opposite. Then he went on to say this:
If Quebec secedes, confederation as we know it will be gone. Western Canada will be on its knees, begging at Washington's doors.
He went on to say this:
We may wake up and find ourselves too late.
I want to direct these remarks to the attention of hon. members opposite, through you, sir, and particularly to those from the province of Quebec:
Mr. Teillet said the crisis Canada now finds itself in has been caused by a complete lack of understanding and communication between French and English speaking Canadians.
Sir, what party in Canadian history has always said that it was the only party that could communicate the hopes and aspirations of French Canada to the rest of the nation? There they sit, and they have their members from the province of Quebec, but in the words of one of their own ministers they have failed to communicate the hopes and aspirations of their people to this parliament and to Canadians from other parts of this nation. I ask you, sir, is this the kind of represen-

tation that the people of any area have to expect from those they send to parliament? For more than half a century, with the exception of a few years, la belle province has sent to the parliament of this nation those majorities that should have been compelling in persuasion, in understanding, in the translation of those problems dear to the hearts of their people, and yet only a few short weeks ago 16,000 farmers from the province of Quebec had to register their disgust with the agricultural policies of this country. Due to lack of action from hon. members opposite, they marched on the capital of their own province. Somebody said they do not get $10 an acre. We never got $10 an acre in western Canada. I remember a prime minister who told the people of Quebec: Elect us, and we will do for you what John Diefenbaker did for western Canada.
Out of order.

If I am out of order it is because of the interruptions from across the way.
I recall that a delegation came down from western Canada. We did not give them all they asked but we tried to place legislation on the statute books the benefits of which they could share together with the rest of the farmers of this nation, and I am proud to see sitting in this place one who was responsible for this achievement to a greater degree than any other Canadian in recent history- the minister of agriculture of that day, the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton).
National unity means not only symbols but the tangible things that touch the every day living of Canadians. There never was a government which came to office with so many answers, or a government which took so little action, as the present administration. Once again tonight hon. members opposite have shown by the way they have voted that they would prefer to listen to this debate than admit they have no legislation ready to bring before parliament.
Earlier, I quoted some observations by members of the cabinet. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) is not here tonight; I understand he has a reason for not being present. I believe he told us that he did not know what the people of Quebec wanted.
Oh, oh.

That is what he said. Behind him he has supporters galore. Apparently they have not been able to reach the cabinet, either. I see the hon. member for St. Law-rence-St. George (Mr. Turner) in his place.

This is what he had to say on one occasion. He condemned what he termed-
-the "monopoly of information" and charged that the bureaucracy-"that mandarin class of faceless experts, protected by the cloak of anonymity of a government department, operating beyond the range of the people's control"-is fighting a running battle with members of parliament.
"The M.P.", he said, "is losing that battle with the civil service."
I do not hear him denying he ever said that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: I did not realize the hon. member was so well read.
You do now.
That was your contribution to this flag debate.

That quotation tells a tremendous story. It is the story of what is happening in this parliament today. Backbenchers are not doing their job, or else the Prime Minister would never have placed before us the measure which the country does not want and which many of his own supporters do not want. They say that we on this side are engaged in a filibuster. We are said to be obstructing. But you, Mr. Speaker, know that debate is the life of parliament. You know, too-
Not debate-legislation.
Bring it in then.
The hon. member had an opportunity tonight but he would not grasp it. His leader would not grasp it either. What I wanted to say was this-those interruptions almost got me off the track.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: They almost got you on to it.

The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George revealed something which has been reiterated by backbenchers across the way on more than one occasion. In debate, when one is faced with a proposition which is not only threatening the unity of this nation but destroying it, what else can an opposition do but take a course such as we are following tonight? No one would say that a plebiscite is the first answer to this question. But no one would say, either, that the Canadian people should not be consulted now, in view of the division which has appeared in almost every part of this country. This is why I feel so strongly that we should give consideration to the subject matter of the subamendment and of the amendment.
Before I pass on to deal with other matters, I have some clippings here.
Canadian Flag
Oh, oh.

I know I have a few here tonight, but they do not amount to 132,000, the number received by the Secretary of State (Mr. Lamontagne) in regard to this proposition, as he told us in answer to a question. I have a telegram here from a zone rally of the Royal Canadian Legion as follows:
Recent Legion zone rally respectfully urges continued support red ensign.
Here is another:
The Royal Canadian Legion at its 20th biennial convention in Winnipeg overwhelmingly endorses the Canadian red ensign and asks your unqualified support of its stand.
I have another here from the Royal Canadian Legion, Saskatoon. This was sent to me during the period when Saskatoon was without a member:
In view of the fact that at present there is no sitting member for the Saskatoon constituency the members of our branch request that you give your consideration to the following resolution-
Perhaps I should read the resolution. This is the way they put it:
Resolved that we urge delay in the proposed legislation for the adoption of the new flag and propose retention of the red ensign as Canada's flag until more assurance is obtained that this legislation has the concern of the nation.
Is there a single member on the other side of the house who would argue that they have the consent of the nation when they put forward this resolution? They are a minority in a house of minorities. They received a minority of the votes in the last general election. They have completely reversed the stand taken by the order in council put forward by one of their own former prime ministers. When I read the debates of those days I find tremendous arguments which could be used against the adoption of a resolution such as they are now trying to put through the house.
Order. The time allotted to the hon. member has expired.

I had
not intended to take part in the debate at this point. However, we have passed a great many days on this single issue, and tonight we had a vote. For my part I voted against the motion that the debate be adjourned. Why did I do that?
Tell us.

I will tell you why. I do not know whether the Conservatives are getting a little fed up. I would just as soon see them with their tongues sticking out, if they expect

Canadian Flag
to bring into the house a series of amendments. Let them bring in one amendment, with one flag proposition, and let us have the vote. I am willing to have a vote on it and we in this corner of the house have been taking this stand since the beginning.
You have been sitting on your hind end.

I may have been, as one hon. member has said, sitting on my hind end. That may be perfectly true, but I still think that is more useful than what he is trying to do. This country and this house wants a flag; there is no doubt about that. We have now spent 20 days on the flag debate. If we did not want a flag, we would look pretty silly at the moment all across the country in every province. People are wondering what is wrong with this parliament. They ask "What are they trying to do? What are they trying to prove? They look like a bunch of school kids that has lost its teacher". You just cannot go around blaming the people, blaming this guy or that guy.
We will blame you now.

But you can blame some Liberals and their past administration, and some Conservatives and their past administration. We have had these two parties sitting in this house as the government for practically a century. The mess we are now in has been built up by nobody else but them. We have heard a great deal about this flag debate, Mr. Speaker. People have been waiting a long time for this flag. But they do not want the flag brought in through disunity and misery; they do not want a flag that will tear this country apart. Right now this issue is tearing the country apart. Perhaps the leader of the Liberal party, the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) is as much to blame for this as anybody else because he has been too much of a fancy skater; he has tried too much to save the goat and the cabbage at the same time. But perhaps the greatest separatist we have in this country right now sits on the front bench as Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) in this house. When I hear the Leader of the Opposition-
On a point of order, Mr. Speaker-
-say in this house-
Order. The hon. member for Edmonton East on a point of order.

On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, I submit that the last remark of the hon. member for Megantic (Mr. Langlois) should be withdrawn. That is a complete falsehood and should not be accepted by this house. I insist that it be withdrawn because it is an irresponsible statement.
I understand perfectly the feelings of the hon. member for Edmonton East, but all hon. members have an opportunity to give an explanation or an answer, in subsequent debate, to a statement like that.
Nobody will pay any attention when they know where it came from.
Mr. Speaker, is the word used by the hon. member for Megantic in reference to the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) parliamentary?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext: Sure.
These questions are, of course, not easy to answer. I would say that the word used was rude; but in my opinion it was not unparliamentary.
I agree with you, Mr. Speaker. It was indeed very rude and shows the ignorance of the hon. member.
Hear, hear.
I know perfectly well that the word was rude, but the truth is often difficult to accept.
It is a scurrilous lie.

Just to prove my point, Mr. Speaker, when we hear a man such as the Leader of the Opposition, who is before the eyes of the people of this country just as much as the Prime Minister himself, go out in this country and say that the three maple leaf flag is a major concession to Quebec, I will not accept that statement; Quebec will not accept it, and Canada will not accept it, from the Leader of the Opposition or anybody else.

On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member has made a statement to the effect that the Leader of the Opposition has said that the three maple leaf flag is a massive concession, or a concession, to Quebec. That is also a falsehood. Those words were never used by the Leader of the Opposition.
Hear, hear.
But they were used by his supporters.

Order. A little earlier today I counselled one hon. member to stop referring to another hon. member in the house in his general argument. It is a matter of courtesy and custom that, while you may attack a political party, its politics, its activities and all the rest of it, one does not launch an attack on the leaders of particular parties. We are here to discuss general principles, and not personalities.
I agree with you in that respect, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Withdraw the remark.
It is not the personality or his integrity that I want to attack. I attack the man, as leader of a party and representing a philosophy, if they have one-

It isn't funny money, that's for sure.
Business of the House

I am not attacking the man as a man, as the hon. member for Prince Albert in his personal life, or anything like that; that is certainly not my intention. I am attacking the man as the representative of the party and the spokesman for that party, normally.
Well, stay with the facts.
Order, please. It is now 10.30.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I ask whether the order of business for tomorrow holds as announced?

Yes, Mr. Speaker.
At 10.30 p.m. the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to special order.
